#4493. Endangered, colorful garter snakes released into the wild for the first time

Published Nov 12, 2026 4:08 PM EST

Most people have never seen a San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia). Native only to California’s San Mateo and Santa Cruz counties, the brilliantly colored reptile was one of the initial entries in the United States Fish and Wildlife Service’s first endangered species list in 1967. After nearly 60 more years of droughts, invasive species, disease, low genetic diversity, and poaching, researchers estimate only a few thousand San Francisco garter snakes still exist in the wild.

However, conservationists recently scored a major win for the snakes. For the first time, 62 of young serpents born at the San Francisco Zoo were released at specific sites across San Mateo County earlier this fall. The successful rewilding of dozens of the endangered snakes marks a huge moment for population rehabilitation efforts, and hopefully clears the way for similar releases in the future.

“Seeing these young snakes returning to the wild represents years of research, collaboration, habitat restoration and careful conservation work,” Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District (Midpen) biologist Karine Tokatlian said in a statement. “This first release is an important step toward building healthy, resilient populations that can sustain themselves over the long term.”

Although slender, the brightly colored San Francisco garter snake can grow anywhere from 18 to 55 inches long. Its eyes are larger than most of its fellow garter snakes, allowing it to keep active during daylight hours. With no fangs and only mildly toxic saliva, the snake is essentially harmless to humans, although its bites are fatal for prey like smaller reptiles and rodents.

The process of releasing young animals like these snakes that were reared in captivity is known as head-starting. It is an effective way to protect creatures during the most vulnerable stage of their lives. Head-starting the first batch of San Francisco garter snakes began in 2025, when conservationists collected multiple pregnant females from a healthy preserve in California’s Midpeninsula. Researchers later released the adult snakes back into their habitats after they gave birth, but kept the infants at the San Francisco Zoo. While there, zoologists conducted genetic testing on each snake to select the best possible locations for their eventual release. Conservationists deposited about one-third of them in the same area as their mothers, then placed the other two-thirds at locations particularly in need of greater genetic diversity pools for breeding.

As biologists continue to monitor the first generation of head-started snakes, another generation is already waiting for its time to shine. More than 130 garter snakes have been born at the San Francisco Zoo this year alone, with an eye to release them sometime in 2027.

“This species is special in many ways, but unfortunately its critical status is not unique,” added Midpen wildlife ecologist Ariel Starr. “The success of this project and the associated research will not only benefit the San Francisco garter snake but will also hopefully inform the recovery of many imperiled reptile species.”

#4492. Meta to deploy 25 electric semi trucks across I-10 corridor, but has nothing to ship

Electric truck operator Nevoya is expanding its deal with Meta with the fresh deployment of 25 Class 8 battery-electric trucks on the Interstate 10 (I-10) between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona … but Meta won’t be shipping any products.

The second major trucking deal between Facebook parent company Meta and electric truck operator Nevoya will put 25 new battery-electric semis on I-10, running freight between San Bernardino, California and Phoenix, Arizona. But Meta isn’t buying trucks, hiring drivers or shipping its own products. Instead, Zuck’s company helping pay for someone else’s cleaner freight through environmental attribute certificates (EACs), a carbon credit mechanism that lets companies claim the emissions benefits of electric trucking without operating the trucks themselves.

“Coming back to Nevoya for a second corridor reflects what we look for in our value chain work: partners that can scale, and agreements we can repeat, said Devon Lake, Head of Net Zero Strategy, Meta. “Freight is part of the emissions footprint of building and operating our data centers, and multi-year commitments like this help address our scope 3 emissions and make electric trucking available and competitive on the routes that serve the regions where we build.”

Meta was one of several buyers in the DC-based Center for Green Market Activation (GMA) buyers’ alliance. The group’s collective EAC purchases supported Nevoya’s initial 63-truck deployment on the Houston–Dallas corridor back in May. This new Agreement, however, is a standalone deal between Nevoya and Meta only, and gives Meta an established framework to open more electric truck corridors in the future.

This clever application of these agreements is what makes the Dallas-Houston run stand out, with GMA calling it, “the first large-scale application of book and claim to zero-emission trucking.” The company adds that this arrangement helps client companies overcome existing barriers to EV adoption while enabling Nevoya to deploy new trucks, “where they deliver the strongest commercial and operational value.”

#4491. Apple HomeView smart home hub review: Siri gets a swanky new house

Published Nov 12, 2026 6:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

Apple’s $299 smart display has been sitting on my kitchen counter for about a week. It looks like a hybrid between an old-school iMac and a giant Apple Watch, but it’s a dedicated home for the recently revamped Siri. It’s an easy addition for anyone already committed to Apple gear. If your smart home runs on cameras, locks, or sensors that don’t work with Apple Home, though, you’ll want an upgrade plan before you buy one.

The HomeView comes in two versions, and both cost $299 in the US. I tested the tabletop model, which mounts a 7-inch square touchscreen on a domed aluminum speaker base and includes a 30W power adapter and USB-C cable in the box. You can have it in any color you want, as long as it’s silver, starlight, rose pink, or space gray. The Apple HomeView (Wall Mounted) drops the base and its extra speaker hardware, as well as the starlight/rose pink color options, and the panel costs more to put on a wall than its sticker price suggests. It requires a Schneider Home mount sold separately, and those start at $59.95. The cheapest USB-C mount also needs a power adapter of at least 20W, which you’ll have to supply yourself.

The HomeView looks the way you’d expect an Apple product to look. Once you take off the protective coverings, the 2.1-pound, 6.82-inch tall device is pretty right out of the box. And it looks great between a breadbox and a butcher’s block, especially compared to an older smart screen that I’ve had there for years, which looks ancient next to it. A stainless steel hinge connects the screen to the base, so you can tilt the display toward wherever you’re standing. The screen stays firmly in place after you position it, even if you tap aggressively like I tend to. It doesn’t wobble or shake as you navigate on-screen menus.

Setting up the HomeView feels like setting up an iPhone or any other recent Apple device. It requires an iPhone running iOS 27.2 or later (or an iPad on iPadOS 27.2), so if your phone isn’t there yet, like mine wasn’t, you’ve got to stop and run the update first. The HomeView played a soft, heavenly drone the whole time it waited, which is a much nicer way to sit through a software update than staring at a progress bar. Also, when you first boot things up, you might think you can immediately start asking for the kind of stuff you ask Siri on your iPhone, but you may have to go through a round or two of launching apps on the HomeView to give them permission to access your account even if your iPhone is with you.

The HomeView’s Liquid Retina LED backlit screen has looked great in every lighting condition I’ve put it in. Apple rates the 1088-by-1088-pixel (220 ppi) display’s brightness between 0.3 and 500 nits, and that bottom end is what makes it work on a nightstand. In a dark kitchen, it reads as a soft glow instead of a floodlight.

The multitouch True Tone touchscreen responds quickly, and it kept registering taps even when my fingers were slightly wet (even though the device doesn’t have a specific water-resistance rating). That’s a real advantage for a screen that spends its life in a kitchen.

The new, more conversational Siri AI on the HomeView is a big jump from the old Siri. The HomeView’s four-mic design ensures Siri can hear you from throughout the room and, when a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone is nearby, it can pull from personal data. If you ask about an upcoming concert, it can also check the calendar on your Apple account and tell whether you’re actually free to go.

That personal access runs through the HomeView’s 12MP Center Stage camera. It can recognize up to six Home app-registered household members by face, and it only shows someone’s personal information when it recognizes that person and their paired iPhone or iPad is on the same Wi-Fi network—with support for Wi-Fi 6E (802.11ax) with MIMO—and was recently unlocked. The HomeView’s A18 chip uses what Apple calls Secure Exclaves to process the camera and microphone feeds in a separate compartment, and Apple says neither the operating system nor Apple itself can access it. Those safeguards are reassuring on paper, though they aren’t something I could independently verify while testing a smart display in my kitchen.

That reliance on a nearby iPhone or iPad is also the source of the HomeView’s most frustrating quirk. With my phone on me, Siri sometimes can’t decide which device should answer. The first few times I tried to set a simple timer, it turned into a dance between the HomeView and my phone before one of them finally took the request. It takes a little getting used to.

Your iPhone also supplies a big share of the HomeView’s apps. There’s no App Store on the device. It ships with 15 built-in apps, including Safari, FaceTime, Music, and Home, and it pulls a handful of other Apple apps, like TV and News, from your phone. So, if you don’t mind some severe letterboxing, you can watch TV and movies on there. Supported third-party audio and video apps show up from a paired iPhone, too, through a system that works a lot like CarPlay. If a service you rely on doesn’t support it, there’s no way to install it on the HomeView directly.

The HomeView’s main job is running your smart home, and that’s where my experience was most mixed. It controls accessories you’ve added to Apple Home, which includes supported HomeKit and Matter devices. My Ring cameras don’t integrate with Apple Home natively, so they never appeared in the HomeView’s Home Camera face, which can otherwise show up to nine live feeds at once. It worked easily with my smart lighting and other natively compatible devices.

Check whether your current cameras, locks, sensors, and thermostat show up in Apple Home before you plan to run the whole house from this screen. If they don’t, budget for HomeKit or Matter replacements that do (and Apple has a whole suite of new options developed alongside LG and Schneider Electric).

The actual smart hub interface that displays on screen is handy for keeping tabs on what’s going on in your home. It’s important to note that this thing looks like a thermostat when it’s on the wall, but it isn’t one. Maybe a future model with a built-in thermostat could free up some wall space.

The HomeView turned out to be a great cooking assistant. Once you open a recipe page on the web, either on your iPhone or in Safari on the HomeView, a Start Cooking button reformats it so you can follow the steps in real time while you work. Recipe pages vary wildly in how they’re formatted and coded, and I expected that mess to trip it up. It has worked without a problem every time I’ve used it so far.

I made a fairly simple recipe for peanut butter noodles, and the instructions and timers were helpful and easy to use. More complicated recipes are more of a challenge, especially since you can’t really perform more than one step at a time, so don’t expect it to turn you into Gordon Ramsay overnight.

As for the audio, the tabletop HomeView sounds full for its size. Its base holds a down-firing woofer and two force-canceling passive radiators, almost like a subwoofer in miniature (but without the extension), and the display adds two custom full-range down-firing drivers of its own. I’d been using an older Google smart display before this, and the jump in sound quality is obvious.

In separate tests, PopSci editor Tony Ware spent a couple of nights with his own HomeView and some of his favorite songs and came away with positive impressions. Compared to a HomePod mini, the beat hits more convincingly. While there’s not much room for excursion in the base, output manages to be surprisingly potent without sacrificing clarity. It won’t beat some recent whole-home audio-focused connected speakers (or Apple’s own full-sized 2nd-gen. HomePod, for that matter), but it’s plenty room-filling for such a compact, multipurpose enclosure. Whether you’re chopping carrots or choppin’ it up with friends, the HomeView is more than enough speaker for a smaller space.

What was more impressive was the airy, open presence of Dolby Atmos tracks from Apple Music, given the use of reflections and computational audio rather than an actual array of directional drivers. With accelerometers and Apple silicon adjusting the acoustic system’s EQ and output based on the screen’s tilt, the result is more incisive than immersive … how it will always be when you can’t surround yourself with speakers. Still, it projects clearly without sounding overly bright or edgy, which is good for podcasts to playlists.

There are occasional kinks, however. If you’re into spatial audio, the best way to ensure you’re getting the correct version of a track is to ask the HomeView to pull Apple Music directly from the cloud; sometimes the Dolby Atmos badge won’t pop up when you send a track from your phone over AirPlay, so you can’t be certain it’s not just stereo. Alternatively, you can hand off whatever is playing on your phone by bringing it close enough to the HomeView to get an AirDrop ripple animation and the album art to show up. Also, you might find yourself instinctively running your finger along the edge of the display looking for volume buttons, but there are no physical controls, which isn’t surprising from an aesthetic standpoint but still feels like a shortcoming.

The Apple HomeView makes the most sense on a nightstand, on the wall next to your thermostat, or in the kitchen. Its Photos face turns it into a digital picture frame, which keeps it from looking like a giant Apple Watch stuck to your wall or sitting on your table (though the clock faces are cute and colorful).

If your home already runs on an iPhone and Apple Home accessories, HomeView slots right in and puts it all on one screen you’ll actually want to look at. If you’ve built your smart home around gear that doesn’t work with Apple Home, however, plan to replace it before you make the jump.

#4488. Young sea turtles make an unexpected home in the Gulf of Oman

Published Nov 13, 2026 12:00 AM EST

For one group of young sea turtles, a protected wetland in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) proved a perfect oasis. A team tracking nine juvenile green turtles (Chelonia mydas) found they were spending over 80 percent of their time in the Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area, a human-made lagoon on the UAE’s Gulf of Oman coast. Large numbers of turtles are also found in this basin built beyond the salt-tolerant trees and shrubs along the coast. A study published today in the journal Aquatic Conservation details the findings.

In 2003, the basin was excavated as an extension of the Khor Kalba mangrove trees. The resulting Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah Protected Area has been recognized as a wetland of international importance under the Ramsar Convention and as a Key Biodiversity Area since 2013.

“Our results show just how critical coastal wetlands can be to young green turtles,” Dr. Owen Exeter, a study co-author and marine conservation ecologist from the University of Exeter, said in a statement. “The fact these turtles are using the artificial basin appears to be a happy accident, and an example of how wildlife can find a way in a world increasingly shaped by humans. However, without the natural mangroves connecting to this system, it’s unlikely that this would have occurred.

According to the team, the floor of the basin is covered with algae, which likely means the turtles have enough food. A few sharks are making their way to this habitat.

The turtles are now also showing “strong reliance” in the man-made basin, with five times higher odds of being found there than in surrounding habitats.

While this spot can be a refuge, the natural mangrove channels also play a critical role in connecting the juvenile turtles (those with a shell less than 23 inches across) to the sea. These channels allow them to move with the tides and show the importance of protecting the entire ecosystem, not just parts of it.

“The government of Sharjah currently protects most of this area from building development, fishing and boating—preserving the last mangrove ecosystem on UAE’s east coast,” Exeter said. “Coastal wetlands are tropical nature hotspots, providing essential nursery and foraging habitats for species including sea turtles. Wetlands are among the most threatened ecosystems globally, so we urgently need to understand how key species use both modified and protected wetlands.”

While these findings are positive for the turtles living in the protected area, their life cycle depends on nesting beaches. Many of these beaches have already been lost to coastal development, and fishing, vessel traffic, and pollution affect the other nearby areas.

One of the turtles swam over 430 miles south to central Oman, highlighting the need for conservation management of these mobile species once they are old enough to leave critical wetland sites.

“Overall, our findings show that coastal wetlands, including engineered ones, can provide valuable habitat for juvenile turtles, provided they are designed for ecological connectivity and subsequent human pressures and threats are minimised,” concluded study co-author Brendan Whittington-Jones from the Sharjah Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA) who led the study.

Happily, the R2’s most delightful feature, its power roll-down hatch glass, is standard. Major options included the $1995 Comfort package, which adds ventilated front seats and heated second-row seats, and the $995 towing package (max capacity: 3300 pounds). Plenty of off-road hardware is standard: skid plates, an electronically locking rear differential, and 33-inch all-terrain tires. And because Jeep is leaning into the “Wrangler, but electric” theme, the Recon’s doors and rear windows are removable without tools. But, at about 70 pounds each, the doors might not be removable without a daily swig of creatine.

The R2’s styling is “Honey, I Shrunk the R1.” It’s clean, modern, and employs the signature Rivian ovoid headlights. There’s nothing too revolutionary about it, but that works to its advantage—Rivian wants to sell the hell out of this thing, and divisive styling is not a smart play for conquesting market share from internal-combustion rivals. (Just ask the Tesla Cybertruck.) And, hey, you can’t go wrong with big wheels pushed out to the corners. Our tester had all-season tires on 21-inch wheels, the mall-crawler spec, but Rivian does offer tougher-looking 20-inch wheels with all-terrain tires. Those, however, will drop EPA-rated range from 330 miles to 307 miles.

See all results for new 2026 Jeep Recon EV for sale near 87123

The Recon’s aesthetic is intentionally anti-EV, with nary a concession to aerodynamics or rolling resistance. It’s square, tall, and has a front bumper that looks like a bulldog’s underbite, all of which contributes to an atmosphere-battling 0.404 coefficient of drag. It doesn’t quite pull off the Wrangler’s studied minimalism, but the Recon is the most off-road-forward EV this side of a Hummer or a Mercedes-Benz G580e. It’s also capable of changing up its look, depending on whether the doors and windows are removed. Buttoned up, it’s a regular SUV with an off-road bent, but ditch the doors and open the full-length canvas roof, and it’s like you’re driving something from the car-stripping contest in I’m Gonna Git You Sucka.

Inside, the R2 and Recon represent their respective manufacturers’ design philosophies. Whether you prefer the spare, screen-centric Rivian or the more conventional Jeep is a matter of your priorities (and, maybe, age), but the Recon is undeniably more user-friendly. Stellantis may whipsaw on its product planning—EVs! No, V-8s!—but its interiors are consistently good, from Jeep to Ram to the Chrysler Pacifica. A splash of tan leather across the top of the steering wheel matches the seats, and a red panel on the console draws attention to the rocker switch for the terrain modes. Both the Rivian and Jeep feature large touchscreens, but the Recon augments its touchscreen functions with hard buttons (on both the dash and the steering wheel) and knobs for volume and tuning. The Jeep’s Uconnect 5 system also supports wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, while the Rivian doesn’t allow phone mirroring.

Rivian minimizes physical controls in part by aping Tesla’s strategy of forcing scroll wheels into multiple roles. Want to adjust the steering wheel or exterior mirrors? You’ll need to go into a settings menu in the touchscreen and temporarily deputize the steering wheel scroll wheels (“haptic halo wheels,” in Rivian parlance) to handle whichever adjustment you’re pursuing. It’s annoying, but probably not the kind of thing you deal with too often as an owner. At least, while you’re wrestling with that, you can gaze upon the lovely birch trim that spans the dash.

Both interiors allow a view of the sky, with the Rivian employing a fixed panoramic glass roof and the Jeep offering the full convertible experience with its power roll-back soft top. The R2 can also drop its windows (including the back one) with the touch of a button—the rear quarter windows stay fixed, alas. You can remove those in the Recon and, unlike the doors, store them in the car in handy bags. In any case, both SUVs are down with al fresco travel, but the Recon is more committed. The catch is, you’ve got to be committed too.

The Recon and R2 both showcase the hyperbolic performance we’ve quickly come to regard as the EV norm. Why, some of us are old enough to remember when the C5 Corvette Z06’s sub-four-second run to 60 mph was considered wickedly quick. And now we have family off-roaders that will torch that Vette—and plenty of other sports cars besides. To wit: The R2’s dual motors combine for 656 horsepower and 609 pound-feet of torque, good for a 3.5-second 60-mph time and an 11.4-second quarter-mile at 126 mph.

HIGHS: Removable doors and glass, quicker than a Charger Scat Pack, real off-road ability.LOWS: 160 miles of real-world highway range, higher price, Wrangler people will probably leave ducks on it.VERDICT: Jeep’s EV off-roader is fun and fast but far from frugal.

The Jeep is even more powerful, and its huge Nexen Roadian ATX tires are churned by 670 horsepower and 620 pound-feet of torque. The Recon ties the R2 to 60 mph and is slightly behind in the quarter-mile, requiring 11.8 seconds. The Jeep’s quarter-mile time is compromised by its 111-mph speed limiter, which it hits more than a second before it finishes the quarter. And still, it runs 11s. If you’re wondering how quick the Jeep would be minus the doors and glass, superleggera-style, so did we. And we’ll let you know the answer to that next time we get our hands on one.

The Jeep’s 94-kWh battery is bigger than the Rivian’s 88-kWh pack, but the Rivian’s superior efficiency means that it goes longer between charges. In our 75-mph highway range test, the R2 managed 260 miles, a full 100 miles more than the Recon. It also charged a little bit faster, going from 10 to 90 percent charge in 39 minutes, versus 43 minutes for the Jeep. If you’re not doing 75 mph, the Recon fares somewhat better—its EPA-estimated range is 222 miles—but it’s still well short of the 300-mile threshold that’s become a common range expectation for EVs.

Neither the Rivian nor Jeep are particularly impressive dynamically, but as with range, you can divine their handling prowess just by looking at them. On the skidpad, the Jeep holds on for 0.74 g of grip, while the Rivian ekes out 0.81 g. The R2 also out-stops the Recon from 70 mph, 178 feet to 201 feet. We’d guess both those differences would be narrowed if the Rivian wore its available all-terrain tires, but both machines are like old-school muscle cars—hellaciously quick in a straight line but not about to hang with a Mazda Miata in the corners.

Although our two contenders here are calibrated more for on-road comfort than apex-slaying performance, the Recon is far more competent and composed than the Wrangler that it’s cosplaying as—an independent front suspension and rack-and-pinion steering work wonders to modernize the Jeep driving experience. It’s tall, yes, but you don’t get the sense that you’re heaving around in the crow’s nest of an 18th-century schooner, nor does it impart the side-to-side neck snap that presents when overly aggressive anti-roll bars begin asserting themselves. The cushy ride is helped by the all-terrain tires’ generous 70-profile aspect ratio. You won’t likely bend a Recon rim on a pothole or a rock out on the trail.

HIGHS: Stupidly quick, looks great inside and out, the rear glass rolls down!LOWS: Lack of physical controls, light regen setting still too strong, no CarPlay or Android Auto.VERDICT: A premium SUV for the masses that happens to be electric.

Many of us feel the R2 is better to drive than its big sibling, the R1S, despite having a simpler suspension setup with conventional anti-roll bars. The R2 feels like it had plenty of R&D attention, in accordance with its importance to Rivian’s business model. Specifically, the spring and damping rates feel in harmony, with firm body control but enough compliance to soak up nasty pavement. There’s no sense of the suspension abruptly running out of travel, either on droop or compression.

Both the Recon and R2 feature some mandatory brake regeneration when you back off the accelerator, but the Recon’s is milder and feels more like coasting compared to the Rivian’s system. Rivian really wants you to embrace one-pedal driving—in fact, it insists. We’re still not sure why Rivian is so big on mandatory regen, but if you like your car to coast down hills (which, as we’ve explained before, is more efficient than converting kinetic energy to electricity and back again), then the R2 might be a little too one-pedal for you even in its weakest mode.

We didn’t get to really off-road the R2 and Recon, but that contest might be closer than you’d think. The Jeep takes its off-road mission seriously, with 9.1 inches of ground clearance and those 33-inch tires, but the modest Rivian actually has more ground clearance (9.6 inches), and its 32-inch tires aren’t much smaller. Speculatively, they’d both be fun to take muddin’.

The Recon is quick and charismatic, but its high price and stunted range make us think that Jeep built this model as an EV beachhead rather than as a serious volume contender. It’s also better at being a Jeep than it is at being an EV. If you wanted an electric Wrangler, this is the closest thing to it, for now. You can drive it in Mad Max dune-buggy mode, and strangers will leave ducks on the windshield, but the Recon is a fun idea that’s desperately awaiting the next generation of batteries to extend its range. Put it this way: When you’re shelling out more than $70K, it hurts to get smoked on range by the $29,000 Chevy Bolt (262 miles, per the EPA).

So the R2 wins this contest because it delivers the design—and most of the performance—of the R1S at a much lower price point. It’s easy to build a compelling vehicle when you’re charging more than $120,000 (see: the R1S Quad), but it’s much more impressive when you’re targeting the high $60,000 range, the heart of the market. With more than 300 miles of EPA-rated range to go with its scalding acceleration, the R2 is the electric family SUV we’d want to put in our own driveway.

#4486. The Sanrivatti One Supercar Has an 800-HP Judd V-10 and a Motorcycle-Like Seating Position

If you were looking for something different from the norm ... this Dutch supercar sure does different.

There’s a new supercar company out of the Netherlands that, apparently, thinks the orientation we typically sit in to drive is out of style. It asks, what if your head was forward of your legs? And, what if you were kneeling as opposed to sitting? Strange, yes—but now such a machine exists. The car in question is called the Sanrivatti One, and the Dutch startup just revealed all the details.

The seating position, which you can check out below, is but one of the unique selling points (or disqualifying features) of the Sanrivatti One. All of the bits around the driver seem more likely to please folks. It has a mid-mounted 5.5-liter naturally aspirated Judd V-10 that makes 800 horsepower and 516 pound-feet of torque, and peak horsepower is produced at a beautiful 9000 rpm. There’s no electrification to be found, and all the power goes to the rear wheels via a Hewland six-speed sequential transmission.

The chassis consists of a carbon fiber monocoque, while a double-wishbone pushrod suspension keeps the 2425-pound car in balance. (Mind you, that quoted weight is dry weight, so expect the final curb weight to be higher.) Braking is handled by AP Racing carbon discs with six-piston calipers in both front and rear. Sanrivatti fits Michelin slick tires from the factory, making it a track-only affair. Said tires wrap 18-inch forged magnesium alloy wheels.

Acceleration figures aren’t available, but the Dutch company claims a 205-mph top speed. Its funky design and aero helps that effort, as Sanrivatti says the exterior is inspired by both the peregrine falcon and a fighter jet. The falcon can be seen in the single sweeping character line that seems to mimic a falcon’s wing in a dive; meanwhile, the single-piece canopy and nose-positioned intakes aim to evoke the aircraft. There’s a large wing that rises up and out from the diffuser, and the majority of the rear is otherwise left open to help dissipate heat from that big V-10.

Meanwhile, here’s what the company has to say about that wild driving position. “Creating an exceptional hypercar is difficult enough,” says Paul Arkesden, executive director of technology partnerships at Sanrivatti. “Creating one around an entirely different driving position means rethinking the relationship between packaging, structure, aerodynamics, ergonomics and controls from the outset. That is what makes the One so interesting.”

The final form of this seating position is similar to what you might experience on a motorcycle, so those who ride could find some familiarity there. Sanrivatti claims it offers about 3.2x better visibility than competitor supercars and track cars. And in case you were worried about being deeply uncomfortable (we sure are), Sanrivatti says it’s developing “proprietary body-support and control technologies” that “allow the driver to move more naturally with the vehicle while remaining supported and secured.”

While today marks the full public debut of the One, it’s still deep in testing stages, with track testing and prototype builds to come. There’s no target date for delivery as of now, so we’ll just need to wait and see what comes our way from Sanrivatti.

#4485. 2027 Acura Integra Type S Turns Back the Clock with New Retro Theme

Acura spruces up its sport compact and celebrates turning 30 with a special edition inspired by one of its most iconic cars.

When Acura revived the Integra nameplate several years ago, it heralded the return of one of the brand’s most iconic models. When the more powerful Type S variant joined the party, Acura could finally offer a true performance-focused car for the first time in years. The new Integra Type S also brought back memories of the legendary DC2 Type R that was sold in America from 1997–2001. For the 2027 model year, Acura is celebrating its 30th anniversary by paying homage to that classic with a new Integra Type S Heritage Edition.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 94043

Before we get into the details about the Heritage Edition, let’s talk about the changes Acura has made to the standard ‘27 Type S. Every example now features gloss-black 19-inch wheels and mirror caps, and the Brembo-branded brake calipers are now painted yellow. There are no powertrain changes, so a rowdy 320-hp 2.0-liter turbo four and sweet-shifting six-speed manual transmission still feed the front wheels.

Inside, Acura now makes the door-panel trim, door handles, and shift boot dark gray, and that applies to the dashboard too, which also adopts a new diamond pattern. The three knobs that control the climate settings are now all gloss black, and Acura says it has redesigned the upholstery options. The Red and Orchid (white) themes feature faux-suede accents that are black and blue, respectively, but the Ebony option features yellow stitching, which extends to the steering wheel, door panels, and shift boot. The driver’s seat now has memory settings, as does the brake-hold feature, and both exterior mirrors tilt down when the car is put into reverse.

If you missed your chance to buy a Phoenix Yellow Integra Type R back in the day, Acura is turning back the clock and giving you another shot. Sure, the new Type S model has an extra pair of doors and put on some weight, but it remains one of our favorite driver’s cars, and the Heritage Edition is the only way to get the new Blazing Phoenix Yellow paint job (at least for the ‘27 model year). Not only is the new retro-themed Type S the first Integra with yellow paint since the 2001 Type R, but it also features exclusive copper-colored wheels. Its interior color is limited to the black-and-yellow theme offered on other new Type S models, but the Heritage Edition alone has a titanium shift knob—same as the Honda Civic Type R.

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 94043

Acura says the 2027 versions of the Integra Type S will reach dealerships sometime next month. While that includes the new Heritage Edition, it’s limited to just 700 examples for U.S. audiences. For those who are lucky enough to score one, it’s only $2300 more than the regular Type S, which starts at $55,995.

Eric Stafford’s automobile addiction began before he could walk, and it has fueled his passion to write news, reviews, and more for Car and Driver since 2016. #4484. Intelligent Speed Limiter Company President: We Don’t Want Our Devices in Every Vehicle in America

Michael Travars sees active intelligent speed limiters as a corrective tool, not a long-term solution.

Michael Travars, president of active roadway safety technology company LifeSafer, has worked for decades to save lives on the road. From ignition interlocks to intelligent speed limiters, Travars has spent his career piloting technology that reduces injuries and deaths in cars. But even this highly safety-conscious executive doesn’t believe in a statewide or federal speed limiter mandate.

Intelligent speed assistance devices have become a hot topic of discussion among municipal governments and car enthusiasts alike in recent years. The European Union mandated that all new cars feature passive ISA systems, which acoustically alert drivers when they exceed the speed limit, in 2024. In the United States, states like New York and cities like Washington, D.C. are piloting programs that require so-called “super speeders” (who have been found guilty of extreme speeding) to install active ISA systems, which prevent lead-footed drivers from exceeding the limits altogether. LifeSafer is working closely with these municipalities to hone the technology—but Travars’s vision of expansion is somewhat limited.

“We don't want this in every car. We actually don't want the European mandate of ISA in every single vehicle. There's a freedom of the road culture here. I'm a big believer in that,” Travars said to Road & Track. “We think a lot about the ignition interlock programs. The ignition interlock program reinforces that you don't drive drunk. It doesn't let you drive drunk. The theory behind those programs is that it creates a habit. You can't drive with alcohol. At the end of the program, the ignition interlock device comes out, and they go back to normal driving programs.”

Using the ISA device is fairly simple. A small screen is mounted on the dashboard, wired through the vehicle’s OBDII port, and operates with a GPS database of roadway speed limits. The device prevents the vehicle from exceeding the posted limit, with a programmable margin of a few miles per hour over said limit. Travars said the devices cost around $6 per day to operate. The device can be overridden, and it includes an RPM-limiting feature that softens typical acceleration.

“There's a tuning process. Actually, if you've done race car driving, it's a lot like tuning a race car, where you connect configuration tools. You actually put the car in neutral. You push the gas pedal all the way down. It measures the rate of acceleration,” Travars explained. “It is a calibration or a tuning process to do the install. And it's more than just OEM or model-specific. It's actually car-specific. A worn-down accelerator pedal has different movement than a modern accelerator, so it is absolutely a car-by-car process.”

LifeSafer ISA currently has three primary customers: teens, fleets, and super speeders. Instead of merely monitoring teenage drivers through apps like Life360, some parents are taking action to limit the ability of their newly minted drivers to speed. Fleet operators enjoy similar benefits, including a theoretical increase in efficiency on speed-limited vehicles. But the future of the technology, arguably, is in providing compliance devices for governments.

Virginia has little tolerance for speeding, and the commonwealth was the first state to join forces with LifeSafer earlier this year. As of July 2026, certain reckless drivers are required to install an intelligent speed assistance device under the administration of the Commission on Virginia Alcohol Safety Action Program. And Virginia isn’t the only state in conversation with LifeSafer, either; Travars said seven states—Hawaii, Illinois, Arizona, Maryland, New York, Virginia, and Georgia—have implemented super speeders laws, and around 17 states in total have reached out to the safety technology company.

But Travars said he believes the state and city level should be the ceiling for these devices. While the safety technology industry would benefit from federal regulatory goalposts, Travars explained, the implementation of speed limiters is better suited to state-by-state needs.

“I would love to see federal minimum guidelines as to, what the device must do, how many miles it must be accurate for, a certification process; those kinds of things belong at the federal level. At the state level, what kind of program do you want? How long do you want it for? Who goes in it? Let Maryland do Maryland,” Travars said.

When asked why enthusiasts shouldn’t worry about ISA programs, Travars explained that driving culture in the United States differs greatly from Europe or other markets where widespread ISA programs have been implemented. These devices aren’t meant to limit drivers who have proven themselves to be responsible. Instead, LifeSafer wants these devices to be a temporary stop on the road to safer driving habits.

“Active ISA devices are targeted programs specifically for drivers who need them. These are inexperienced drivers or drivers who have shown that they have a speeding habit that needs to be broken. Period. We don't want ISA in all vehicles. We don't want this to be a mandate in all cars. The goal is to take people who are unsafe drivers, make them safer, and then take them out of the program and restore their right to drive,” Travars said. “These aren't traps. These aren't the [devices] where they report to insurance companies to increase your rates. The data is not sold to third parties ... I think these programs should bar the right to sell that data. These are not trackers. These are not Big Brother. These are meant to serve a specific purpose, which is to reinforce safe driving behavior long enough that it becomes a habit. Full stop.”

A New York transplant hailing from the Pacific Northwest, Emmet White has a passion for anything that goes: cars, bicycles, planes, and motorcycles. After learning to ride at 17, Emmet worked in the motorcycle industry before joining Autoweek in 2022 and Road & Track in 2024. The woes of alternate side parking have kept his fleet moderate, with a 2014 Volkswagen Jetta GLI and a BMW 318i E30 street parked in his Queens community.

#4483. Here are the coolest e-motorcycles and gear we saw at EICMA 2026

Every year, the world’s largest motorcycle companies (and plenty of the world’s smallest motorcycle companies, too) converge on Milan, Italy for Europe’s premier motorcycle showcase. That means that all of the newest electric motorcycle announcements happen in one place, and we get a chance to check out the coolest developments and most interesting new gear.

Below is a list of the best things I saw while walking around the show this year, presented in no particular order.

LiveWire came to EICMA with perhaps its most diverse electric two-wheeler lineup yet, showing just how far the company has expanded beyond the premium electric motorcycles that originally defined the Harley-Davidson spin-off.

The new S4 Honcho family was a major focus, including the street-oriented Honcho Street, off-road Honcho Trail, and newly unveiled Honcho Skate, a stripped-down addition to the modular platform. The booth also included LiveWire’s larger S2 electric motorcycles, creating a pretty broad spectrum from lightweight urban machines up through full-size highway-capable electric motorcycles.

The other big piece of the booth was DUST Moto, which LiveWire acquired earlier this year. The production-intent DUST Hightail was displayed alongside the newly revealed DUST Spur, giving LiveWire an immediate presence in the increasingly popular lightweight electric dirt bike category.

Add in STACYC’s electric balance bikes for young riders, and the entire booth almost looked like an electric two-wheeler progression chart: start a kid on a STACYC, move up through lightweight DUST and Honcho machines, and eventually graduate to a full-size LiveWire.

GR1T Motorcycles is a relatively young European electric motorcycle startup that caught my eye at EICMA with its G1 platform, a lightweight electric motorcycle designed and engineered in Italy. The basic recipe is pretty compelling: 130 km/h (81 mph) top speed, 11 kW of continuous power and 26.6 kW (36 hp) peak, all while weighing just 130 kg (287 lb).

Perhaps most importantly for urban riders, its roughly 6 kWh battery is actually split into two removable 3 kWh packs, meaning apartment dwellers can pull the batteries out and charge them inside. They’re big, but removing them is doable.

GR1T’s bikes therefore pack in around 50% more battery capacity than most electric motorcycles in this size and weight class, meaning roughly 50% more range, as well.

There are also some interesting and clever design choices, like the underslung rear suspension and the triple-camera system that includes front and rear dashcams plus a cockpit-facing camera for recording the rider.

The clever part of the overall design scheme is that GR1T isn’t developing a separate platform for every motorcycle. The same basic G1 chassis, motor, batteries, belt drive, and electronics underpin four versions: the G1S Street, G1X Scrambler, G1XR Raider, and utility-oriented G1M Mission.

Prices are set to start at €8,495 including VAT, putting these squarely in that emerging category of reasonably affordable, lightweight electric motorcycles that have enough speed for real-world commuting without chasing superbike performance.

There’s an important caveat, though: these aren’t production motorcycles yet. GR1T says it is currently fundraising, with factory development and pre-orders set to follow after funding closes and first deliveries now targeted for the first half of 2028.

So the bikes aren’t quite ready for primetime yet, but it’s definitely a company to watch.

Real Motors brought one of the more visually striking electric motorcycles to EICMA with Project: ARES, a futuristic electric café racer that the American startup describes as an “Electric Analog” machine – basically an attempt to preserve the raw, mechanical connection of motorcycling while ditching unnecessary screens and gadgetry.

And there’s plenty of performance underneath the sci-fi bodywork: Real Motors lists a 75 kW (100 hp) motor, a 15 kWh battery, a 120 mph (192 km/h) top speed, and an estimated weight of 485 lb (220 kg).

The analog analogy is spot on, with the display probably the simplest and most straightforward I’ve ever seen on an electric motorcycle. There’s also no app, no subscription, and no digital handcuffs. The bike is very much the electric equivalent of a simple ICE bike that just rides, albeit with a much nicer ride.

Unlike many of the futuristic concepts scattered around EICMA, ARES is actually headed toward limited production.

Real Motors plans to build just 250 examples in its first LOT 01 production run, with pricing starting at $20,000 and North American deliveries targeted for early 2027. European deliveries are expected after homologation is completed.

The company has also brought former LiveWire CTO Vance Strader onto the project as it makes the difficult transition from a very cool prototype into an actual production motorcycle.

I actually had the chance to do a spin on the bike, and so I’ll be reporting back on the experience. But you can tell from my smile below that the ride was quite an experience!

Seatylock has been my go-to e-bike lock company for several years now, and I use their locks for my several e-bikes and my wife’s e-bike too.

Now Seatylock has returned with some even more impressive locks. The company showed off its new Ultra D28 lock, which is both angle grinder-proof and wide enough to lock the wheel of a motorcycle. It solves the problem of how do you make a lock strong enough for a motorcycle but also small and light enough that you can actually carry it with you, unlike a massive chain lock that usually stays where you park your motorcycle overnight.

In the image below, you can see the shackle next to an exposed section demonstrating the diamond coating that essentially destroys angle grinder discs – even diamond coated discs.

The company also has a slightly smaller version of the same lock designed for bicycles.

Both will absolutely destroy even the toughest angle grinder discs. Sure, eventually someone could cut through them, but it may take a dozen discs and by that point the thief has moved on to an easier target.

At EICMA 2026, Royal Enfield continued expanding its electric motorcycle ambitions with its Flying Flea sub-brand, showcasing the scrambler-style motorcycle alongside its growing lineup of lightweight, retro-inspired electric motorcycles.

There were several interesting colorways and customized designs on display, showcasing the Flying Flea’s stylish design.

The new models blend Royal Enfield’s classic design heritage with modern electric technology, targeting urban riders and those looking for a fun, approachable electric motorcycle rather than a high-performance machine.

With distinctive styling, compact proportions, and an emphasis on accessible riding, the Flying Flea lineup represents Royal Enfield’s effort to carve out a place in the emerging market for smaller electric motorcycles while maintaining the character that has made its gasoline-powered bikes so popular.

Yamaha showed off its new NMAX E electric scooter, bringing battery-powered performance to one of the brand’s most recognizable urban scooter families.

Designed as an electric alternative to the popular gasoline-powered NMAX, the new model combines familiar sporty styling with a quiet, low-maintenance electric drivetrain aimed at everyday city commuting.

The NMAX E uses Yamaha’s new compact eAxle powertrain, shared with the larger-wheeled XENTER E, and delivers up to 7.5 kW (10 hp) of peak power, putting it in the 125cc-equivalent class.

With its practical step-through design, automatic operation, and approachable performance, the NMAX E represents another step in Yamaha’s push to electrify its urban mobility lineup, particularly in European markets where scooters are already a popular alternative to cars.

Segway showed off a new vision for safer electric scooters, including its futuristic X Cruiser concept that takes rider protection to a whole new level.

Rather than relying solely on traditional motorcycle safety equipment, the X Cruiser explores automotive-inspired features such as integrated seats with seatbelts, partial enclosures, and even a fully roofed version designed to offer additional protection from the elements.

The concept includes several configurations, ranging from a more conventional open scooter to a partially enclosed design and a fully covered model that looks like a cross between a motorcycle and a tiny electric car. While these designs are still concepts rather than production-ready scooters, they demonstrate how Segway is rethinking two-wheeled transportation by exploring ways to make electric scooters safer, more comfortable, and potentially more appealing to riders who might otherwise be hesitant to trade four wheels for two.

Eli Electric Vehicles took to EICMA 2026 to display its compact Eli Zero electric quadricycle, a tiny two-seat urban EV designed to offer much of the convenience of a car without the size, weight, or expense of a conventional automobile.

With its enclosed cabin, side-by-side seating, and ultra-compact footprint, the Eli Zero offers a practical alternative to larger vehicles for short city trips, combining the weather protection and comfort of a car with the maneuverability and efficiency of a much smaller vehicle.

The company revealed a more powerful L7e-class version of the Eli Zero that it had previously teased, expanding the vehicle’s capabilities beyond its existing L6e configuration. The new Race Edition also pushes the envelope farther with custom interior and a few extra accents to the body.

With growing interest in smaller, more efficient urban transportation, Eli’s presence at EICMA definitely underlined how the show is increasingly embracing electric mobility solutions that go beyond traditional motorcycles and scooters.

NIU showed off its latest lineup of electric scooters, continuing the brand’s push to make battery-powered two-wheelers a practical alternative to gasoline-powered urban transportation. Known for its sleek designs, connected technology, and approachable electric scooters, NIU highlighted models aimed at a range of riders, from everyday city commuters to those looking for more powerful machines capable of keeping up with faster urban traffic.

The company showed off several new models for the 2027 model year, with scooters that combine modern styling with features such as smartphone connectivity, smart security systems, and efficient electric drivetrains, all while maintaining the simplicity and low operating costs that make electric scooters so appealing.

While I didn’t see anything groundbreaking at the brand’s booth this year, the incremental updates look to push new tech features further throughout the brand’s many models, helping more of NIU’s offerings enter that premium level that the company has been known for.

For something a bit wilder, Honda shared its futuristic EV Outlier Concept, an electric motorcycle that explores what two-wheeled design could look like when engineers are freed from the constraints of traditional gasoline-powered motorcycles.

With its long, low-slung profile, radically different riding position, and futuristic bodywork, the EV Outlier looks more like something out of a science fiction movie than a conventional motorcycle. The concept features electric motors integrated into both wheels, giving it two-wheel drive while opening up new possibilities for packaging and weight distribution.

Rather than simply replacing a combustion engine with a battery and motor, Honda used the EV Outlier to rethink the entire motorcycle layout, demonstrating how electrification could lead to entirely new types of riding experiences.

While the bike remains a design concept with no announced production plans, it offers an intriguing glimpse into Honda’s vision for the future of electric motorcycles.

Vespa showed off its next-generation electric scooter lineup at EICMA, including electric versions of the Primavera, Sprint S, and Primavera Tech. While they don’t look radically different, there’s a lot more happening underneath the familiar steel bodywork.

A new Italian-made, rare-earth-free electric motor improves efficiency and performance, while the 45 km/h Primavera and Sprint S now feature removable batteries.

The faster 67 km/h Primavera Tech gets up to 90 km of WMTC range – a 12.5% improvement – along with an updated vehicle management system and more efficient charger.

#4482. Rimac Is Reportedly Ending Nevera Production After Selling Just 71 Cars

The electric hypercar set plenty of records, but it may have come in well under the purportedly planned production run of 190 examples.

Rimac is ending production of its all-electric Nevera hypercar at the end of 2026, Germany’s Auto Motor und Sport reports. And somewhat surprisingly, the same report suggests that just 71 of 190 planned Reveras were built over the course of its production run.

The base Nevera, and its later Nevera R variant, have held a number of records, including the title of world’s quickest car, what was once the EV lap record at the Nürburgring Nordschleife, and a quarter-mile run under 7.9 seconds. Those numbers may not have been enough to make the model a hit with buyers, though. According to the report, 51 of a planned 150 base-model Neveras were built, and 20 out of a planned 40 Nevera Rs reached production.

While the apparent final tally of Nevera production is striking, it is part of a larger pattern of electric hypercars failing to find an audience. The Lotus Evija once competed directly with Rimac’s Nevera, but Lotus has since moved on to a hybrid supercar with V-8 power. Former Rimac stakeholder Porsche once considered its own electric hypercar, only to pivot to an internal-combustion supercar instead. Even as cars like the Tesla Roadster and Yangwang U9 Xtreme make headlines with record-setting stunts, there are questions on whether or not a conventional hypercar buyer would be interested in paying for an EV.

See all results for Rimac Nevera for sale near 29405

Whether or not the Nevera itself was a success, the halo car did succeed in raising Rimac’s profile. Namesake founder Mate Rimac is now fully in charge of Bugatti, and Rimac Technology provides electric powertrain components to major cars like the Porsche 911 Turbo S. As the most significant electric hypercar to reach the market to date—well, perhaps along with the closely related Pininfarina Battista—the few Neveras in private hands represent a major leap forward for both electric performance and the Rimac brand itself.

#4481. Stolen $460,000 Audi Race Car and Trailer Recovered After Brazen London Theft

The racing team principal says he was shown his purloined machine over FaceTime as someone attempted to negotiate a ransom for its return.

When a car is stolen, the thief might take it for a joyride, ship it overseas, or deliver it to a chop shop. Stealing a car and holding it for ransom is considerably less common. And stealing a $460,000 race car before then demanding money for its return? That's a whole different level of unusual. But that's exactly the bizarre situation that apparently recently unfolded in London. According to a BBC report, a British Touring Car Championship (BTCC) Audi was stolen, then someone allegedly contacted the racing team's principal over FaceTime, showed him the stolen car, and attempted to negotiate a ransom for its return.

BTCC team Power Maxed Racing owns the car. On Thursday, the team posted on social media that their racing Audi had been stolen the night before. The car was inside a trailer, and it was parked at the Excel London exhibition center. The lot where it was parked was locked and had on-site security, but apparently that was not enough to keep the brazen thieves at bay.

Power Maxed Racing offered a £25,000 (roughly $33,000) cash reward for the return of the purpose-built racer. However, the story soon took another strange turn. According to the BBC, Power Maxed Racing team principal Adam Weaver got a call "with somebody FaceTiming me showing me the car trying to get the ransom." Weaver reportedly told the person that he needed some time to organize the cash and sleep on the prospect of paying a ransom for the safe return of the car.

Weaver received a much more encouraging call later the same day: the police had found the car and trailer. Both were still in London, and only about 10 minutes away from where they were stolen. Power Maxed Racing went back on social media to share the good news, and to thank everyone who helped spread the word and get the car and trailer back.

In the end, the alleged thieves apparently went through the trouble of breaking into a secure compound and stealing a $460,000 race car, only to have it recovered just down the road. It's unclear whether anyone has been arrested, or if there was any damage to the car or trailer. Fortunately, Power Maxed Racing has its Audi back, and that's what matters most.

#4480. Jeep Is Auctioning Off the Only Copy of the Wrangler 392 Commando Available to Non-Military Personnel

Of the 250 units of the Hemi-powered special edition, 249 went to veterans or active duty U.S. service members. This is the exception.

The Jeep brand has an indelible connection to the U.S. military, even if it has been nearly 60 years since the armed forces actually used a Jeep-branded vehicle. So it wasn’t a huge surprise last year when Jeep announced the wildest factory Wrangler it had yet produced would be called the Wrangler Commando 392.

More surprising was that Jeep had no plans to sell the Wrangler Commando 392 to the general public. Jeep built a limited run of 250 vehicles, and earmarked 249 of them for active-duty service members and veterans. That left only Wrangler Commando 392 available to civilians—and it’s now up for auction on Bring a Trailer. (Usual disclosure: Bring a Trailer, like Road & Track, is part of Hearst Autos.)

The Wrangler Commando 392 is not your typical Jeep Wrangler. As the name suggests, the Commando 392 packs the 6.4-liter Hemi V8 from the still-very-much-alive Wrangler Rubicon 392 and adds a Whipple supercharger for a total of 705 horsepower. (That’s nearly six times the output of the four-pot Wrangler I drove in high school.)

The Commando 392 rides on 37-inch Nitto Ridge Grappler tires, with an internally mounted spare, and 17-inch beadlock-capable wheels. Additional off-road modifications for this Wrangler Commando 392 include a 3.5-inch JKS suspension lift kit, Fox 3.0 internal bypass shocks with remote reservoirs, and a Fox ATS steering stabilizers. It also has a Warn winch and a Magnaflow exhaust system.

Visually, the Wrangler Commando 392 is a bit more sedate. It features a Willys trim-like Army Green paint job, Commando graphics inside and out, and a unique interior trim. The new owner will have to equip the Commando 392 for all-season capability themselves; this Wrangler only comes with the bimini top and tube doors as depicted, not with a hard roof or full-size doors.

The Jeep Wrangler Commando 392 auction will benefit United Service Organizations (USO). If you’re interested, prepare to have your financial ducks in a row as well as your novelty rubber ones; bidding for the only civilian Commando 392 is already up to $100,000 as of this writing, with nine days remaining.

#4478. Slate Is Selling a Road Atlas As a $30 ‘Screenless GPS’ for Its Truck

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

As you can see, it’s literally just a Rand McNally Road Atlas.

Slate Auto is not subtle about keeping its electric truck simple and analog whenever possible. It has hand-crank windows, no carpeting to speak of, and—perhaps most significantly for a car launching in the back half of the 2020s—no central screen. That means navigation duties are probably going to fall to your phone, but Slate is happy to offer another option on its online store. They call it a physical GPS, but you probably know it by another name. The familiar-looking new product available on the Slate website is simply a Slate-branded Rand McNally Road Atlas.

In other words, maps. Slate is selling maps.

Slate built its Truck—that is its official product name—around the idea that a driver will be using their phone for navigation and entertainment, so the Road Atlas offering is mostly a novelty. Still, it is a Slate-branded book of maps covering Canada, Mexico, and the United States. That is useful enough that it might convince one or two dedicated analog buyers to actually choose to navigate their Slate Trucks through the world this way, at least once or twice for the novelty.

The Slate store lists the atlas for $30, and notes that it is “limited edition.” (We will note that the same apparent atlas without the Slate markings and markup costs $19.99 on Amazon.) Slate’s planned products range from starting prices of just under $25,000 to just over $32,000, depending on which of three customizable body styles a buyer picks. Add in $30 for a “Screenless GPS” and you can get yourself across the continent with ease, one 205-mile charge at a time.

#4477. Hyundai is overhauling the Kona, and it looks like it may still be offered as an EV after all

Hyundai is skipping the typical mid-cycle refresh and plans to launch a completely redesigned Kona, with a sleek new style and an updated high-tech interior.

It’s been nearly four years since Hyundai introduced the second-generation Kona, meaning, like most of its models, the compact SUV was expected to receive a mid-cycle refresh.

Hyundai is apparently going straight to the third-generation model instead. Earlier this year, early-stage prototypes were spotted in Korea that looked much boxier and more rugged than the current Kona.

Since then, several test mules have been captured testing in the US, Europe, and other regions, confirming the Kona will adopt a more upright, traditional SUV design similar to the new Santa Fe, Palisade, and Tucson.

The wider, more powerful design appears to draw inspiration from Hyundai’s off-road Crater Concept, revealed at the LA Auto Show last year.

Hyundai said the off-road SUV Concept was a preview of the “next evolution” of its Extreme Rugged Terrain (XRT) vehicles, such as the IONIQ 5 XRT and Palisade XRT Pro. Is the Kona next in line to receive the XRT treatment?

A post shared by SHORTS CAR (@shorts_car)

Apparent leaked images from a few months ago revealed a design that looked like a mashup of the Crater Concept and IONIQ 5, with pixelated lighting and a clamshell hood.

Most recently, the third-gen Hyundai Kona, codenamed “SX3,” was spotted disguised in a parking garage in Korea. The images were sent to ShortsCar, revealing the new Kona’s wheel design.

While earlier reports suggested Hyundai planned to drop the all-electric Kona variant and would only offer gas and hybrid versions, the prototype captured in Korea is expected to be the EV model. However, Hyundai has yet to confirm powertrain or battery specs.

The updates are even more evident on the inside. Previous spy images appeared to show the third-gen Hyundai Kona running Hyundai’s new Pleos Connect infotainment system, like the IONIQ 3.

In the IONIQ 3, Hyundai offers a 12.9″ or 14.6″ center infotainment screen, plus an optional driver display.

Like the current model, the third-gen Kona is expected to be available with fully electric (EV), hybrid, and gas-powered powertrains.

While Hyundai skipped the 2026 Kona EV, the electric version could return in 2027 or 2028 when the third-generation model is expected to arrive.

The hybrid version will likely use the same 1.6L hybrid engine as the new Seltos, while the EV variant could offer similar powertrain and battery options to the IONIQ 3.

The IONIQ 3 is available with two battery packs in Europe and the UK: 42 kWh and 61 kWh, offering WLTP ranges of up to 213 miles (344 km) and 308 miles (497 km), respectively.

#4476. 2027 Acura Integra Type S

See all results for new 2027 Acura Integra Type S for sale near 76259

The Acura Integra Type S is the swankier cousin of the boy-racer Honda Civic Type R. The two share their mechanical underpinnings and hatchback body style, but the Acura is dressed in a more respectable-looking outfit. A lusty 320-hp turbocharged inline-four is under the hood and mates exclusively to a six-speed manual transmission. The combination loves to spin its front tires excitedly, and it's a riot to drive.

An expertly tuned chassis gives the Integra Type S high-spirited handling, and it rides comfortably enough for long trips. The engineers responsible for this gem had driving enthusiasts in mind when this Acura was planned. The cabin is slightly upscale from the Civic Type-R as well, although not as much as you’d think given the six grand price delta between the two.

Expert Tip: Its premium badge and $ 56,000 price tag put the Integra Type S into contention with some European rivals that offer richer accommodations.

Compare the 2027 Acura Integra Type S with the top vehicles in this segment with our new compare tool.

Acura has added a limited-production Heritage Edition to the lineup for 2027. Only 700 will be offered in the U.S., all painted Blazing Phoenix Yellow and wearing special copper-colored aluminum wheels. The Heritage Edition is also emblazoned with black exterior badging and features a titanium shift knob.

The standard Integra Type S gets a few changes for the 2027 model year, too, including new gloss black wheels, yellow brake calipers, dark gray interior trim, and gloss black climate control knobs. Several features have been added as standard, such as memory settings for the driver’s seat and an exterior mirror tilt-down feature that can be set to automatically dip the mirrors when you shift into reverse.

If this year's model is largely unchanged and you're comfortable with a lightly used car, you may want to consider shopping previous model years. A one-to-three-year-old model will likely have a warranty and it'll cost less than buying new.

A 320-hp turbocharged 2.0-liter inline-four with 310 pound-feet of torque is the sole engine for the Integra Type S. Like the Civic Type R, the Integra Type S routes the power exclusively through a six-speed manual transmission and front-wheel drive with a limited-slip differential. Shifter action is wonderfully light and precise—this is one of the best manual shifters in the business—and clutch take-up is smooth and intuitive. With all 310 pound-feet of torque available at 2600 rpm, you could skip a shift or two without worry, but it'd be a shame to miss out on all the fun.

Objectively, roadholding and braking match the Civic Type R, with the Integra Type S pulling 1.02 g's on the skid pad and stopping from 70 mph in just 153 feet. Subjectively, the Civic feels ever so slightly more vivacious from behind the wheel. The Integra Type S knows how to chill in less demanding situations, slipping into an almost-calm cruising mode. All Type S models come with 19-inch wheels wearing summer tires, Brembo brakes, and an exhaust system with three center-mounted exhaust pipes.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

In Comparison: The Integra Type S's brisk 60-mph sprint time is nearly two seconds quicker than the 7.0-second time we posted with the standard six-speed Integra and just 0.2 seconds behind the last Civic Type R we tested.

The EPA estimates that the Integra Type S will deliver 21 mpg city, 28 mpg highway, and 24 mpg combined. It's also worth noting the Type S returned an impressive 31 mpg on our 75-mph highway fuel-economy test, three miles per gallon better than its EPA rating. For more information about the Integra Type S's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

In Comparison: The Audi S3 is slightly more efficient, earning EPA estimates of 23 mpg city and 31 mpg highway, as is the BMW M235 Gran Coupe with estimates of 24 mpg city and 33 mpg highway.

First Row: Acura plays the long game with the Type S's interior, favoring conservative design and quality materials over outright flash. There are plenty of parts shared with the Honda Civic under the skin, but Acura pulls styling elements from its SUVs to foster the familial vibe. Distinctive features include mildly bolstered sport seats upholstered with perforated, faux-suede fabric, “Type S” embossed headrests, and subtle touches including a Type S shift knob, boot, and steering wheel emblem.

Second Row: A pair of individual rear bucket seats and a small center console armrest replace the standard Integra's rear bench. There's room for two in back, but the lack of features such as rear air vents and seat heaters is a notable omission in a supposedly premium car.

Cargo Capacity: Thanks to its Civic roots, the Integra Type S offers the same 24 cubic feet of cargo room accessed via a large hatchback. We fit five carry-on suitcases in the trunk and managed to squeeze in a total of 18 with the rear seats folded.

The Type S gets the same 10.2-inch digital gauge cluster as the rest of the Integra lineup; a 9.0-inch infotainment touchscreen is standard. A wireless smartphone charging pad, a head-up display, and a pair of USB ports are also included. All versions come with a top-tier 16-speaker, 530-watt ELS Studio 3D premium audio system.

A host of driver-assistance features are included as standard in the Integra Type S, including automated emergency braking with pedestrian detection, lane-keeping assist, and adaptive cruise control.

For information about the Integra Type S's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

#4475. Takata Airbag Trouble Prompts New Recall Of 314,000 Toyota And Lexus Vehicles

Aging propellant in certain Takata passenger airbags could cause a rupture during deployment.

The Takata airbag recall scandal started over a decade ago. To date, some 67 million airbags have been included in that series of recalls across dozens of brands. That list is expanding again today, as Toyota is recalling another 314,000 cars in the USA. W

hile the automaker hasn't spelled out exactly which models are part of the recall, owners should consider getting the fix as one of their highest priorities. According to the automaker, the new recall of 314,000 cars affects both Toyota and Lexus products. The company did not break down the make and year models impacted, but the brand says that in all affected vehicles, the issue is consistent with previous Takata recalls. The inflator in the airbag has a propellant inside that can degrade over time due to humidity and temperature fluctuations.

If that inflator ruptures due to that degradation, it can send metal fragments through the airbag and into the cabin. Takata airbags impacted by this issue have injured and killed people over the years. Perhaps the biggest concern is that there is no warning sign of when this might happen.

Toyota says it'll replace the front passenger airbag inflator or the entire assembly depending on the model. While we do not have a make and model list, Toyota does say that owners can cross-check their VIN at Toyota.com/recall or at NHTSA.gov/recalls. In the coming days, we'll likely see the formal documents published by the NHTSA with specifics.

It is worth noting that recalls like this don't necessarily suggest that Toyota was installing faulty airbags recently. According to the NHTSA, 9% of the bad airbags that went out into the automotive population are still out there. That might not sound like much, but that small sliver still accounts for over six million cars. Based on the latest available data, the 2017 Lexus GX460 was the most recent Toyota product included in Takata recalls. Other notable models include the 2008-2014 Lexus IS F, the 2010-2016 Toyota 4Runner, and the 2012 Lexus LFA.

#4473. Peek Inside the Ford Vault, a New Museum Housing the Best From Ford and Lincoln

The Vault will eventually open to public eyes, and it’ll be worth a visit once it does.

For decades, Ford’s internal policy was to not keep examples of cars it’s made. Once their useful lifespan was up, they were to be sold, donated, or trashed. That being the case, there’s never been an official museum of cars past and present operated by the Blue Oval here in the U.S. Until now, that is. Say hi to the Ford Vault.

In the same sense that Porsche has the Porsche Museum and Mercedes-Benz has the Mercedes-Benz Museum, the Ford Vault is a place to admire the long history of Ford and Lincoln. It’s not open to the general public yet – Ford intends to ultimately open its doors to anyone – but we got a sneak preview of what to expect when Ford’s finished with this large hall of vehicles.

As of now, there are 125 cars and trucks inside this warehouse-like building in Romulus, Michigan. Situated about 20 or so miles from Ford World Headquarters in Dearborn, this only exists because of Jim Farley’s blessing. Thanks to orders from the top to change Ford’s vehicle retention policy, a collection of historical vehicles finally became possible. It’s taken about three years of buying special vehicles and unearthing some that were squirreled away, but Ford finally has an array of cars worth showing off. A small fraction of them (about 15 at this stage) are on loan from folks happy to show their cars off in Ford’s space. It’s a practice that Ford says it intends to continue, giving new visitors something fresh to see each time they return.

We got a chance to walk through the Vault this week. Read on for some highlights of what you can expect should you find yourself in the Ford Vault one day.

This Mustang doesn’t look like much from the outside, but it houses one of the most ambitious skunkworks engine projects from Ford that never made it past the prototype phase. Back when Ford was developing the 2005 Ford GT, it was searching for the right powertrain for the job. Engineers thought a V-10 could fit the bill, so it combined two modular 4.6-liter V-8 engine blocks to create a short deck V-10 measuring 351 cubic inches. Hilariously, it fit in the engine bay of the Mustang. This prototype in particular has been kept off the books for decades since to ensure it lived on, and now it’s proudly displayed in the Vault.

Speaking of Ford GTs, the Vault is home to a huge number of them. One of the particularly special ones is this concept that debuted at the 2002 Detroit Auto Show. Nicknamed “Petunia,” it’s an example of a concept that was truly representative of the production car to follow. That said, look close, and you’ll spot the differences. The headlight and fog light designs, for instance, are different on the final car. Same goes for various vents and openings throughout the body. It’s close, but not identical to the 2005 GT that came out a few years later.

The Ka being present here in the Vault foreshadows that it won’t just be American-sold Fords and Lincolns that will make their way into the collection. This particular Ka is the last first-gen example to roll off the line, and it has less than 10 miles on the odometer. It’s also a charming aside from the barrage of Ford Mustangs and GTs on display here.

These three are on loan to Ford for the time being to coincide with the launch of the brand’s new Le Mans Hypercar. As you likely already know, they’re the three GT40s that swept the podium at the 1966 Le Mans. Ford rightly has them lined up in the feature spot inside the Vault. There’s no guarantee these pieces of history will be there when Ford decides to open up to the public, but it sure is a great way to kick this collection off with a bang.

Ford has about 30 different concept cars from across the years on display right now, and one of the funkiest is the Ute Concept. Ford’s EVB Metal Shop crafted this creation using a Ranger bed and the original Mustang decklid as the tailgate. Obviously, it was only ever made as a one-off.

Again, it’s not all Mustangs and GTs, and thankfully, Ford found some space for its affordable, entry-level enthusiast cars. Not pictured here, but across the hall, Ford has both a Fiesta ST and Focus ST on display, too. It’s not often you see perfectly kept Focus and Contour SVTs, so it’s great to see Ford found some to preserve.

It’s not just on-road race cars that made the cut for the Vault, and Ford found a special one with this Baja 1000 Bronco. Prepared by Bill Stroppe for the 1967 Mexican 1000, it’s the first of four Broncos that Stroppe built to compete in off-road rallies and competitions. You might recall its color scheme from today’s Bronco Stroppe Edition made as a tribute to the original truck.

Leno has an absurd number of cars, but did you ever wonder which was his first? That would be a 1934 Ford Pickup, and while the one seen here isn’t the car, it’s an example he bought about 10 years ago to mimic his original. Ford is keeping it safe and dry for Leno for the time being, but it will eventually be shipped back out to California for a future episode of Jay Leno’s Garage.

Ford is seemingly bringing back the Cobra name in a big way soon, and it’s highlighting the trim’s history with a collection of three Cobra Rs here at the Vault. Each one of these Cobra Rs (1993, 1995, and 2000) are the first production examples off the line for each generation. The 2000 Cobra R with its big wing and independent rear suspension is the most well-known of the bunch, and we have high expectations for the continuation of the Cobra line.
