#4360. Tesla Cybercab has crashed 8 times, and the data shows a speed problem

Tesla’s Cybercab now has 8 crashes on file with NHTSA, barely two months after the purpose-built robotaxi started giving public rides in Austin.

Four happened in driverless “Robotaxi” service, and none topped 5 mph. The other four happened with a test driver on board and Tesla’s driver-assist engaged, including one where a Cybercab hit a car at 53 mph on a highway in Philadelphia.

The data points at what we think is the biggest limitation of Tesla’s self-driving program right now: speed.

Tesla files Cybercab crashes under NHTSA’s Standing General Order in two separate datasets.

The first is the ADS (Automated Driving System) file, which covers Level 4 driverless operation. That’s the Robotaxi service, where nobody is in the driver’s seat. NHTSA’s latest ADS release, published this month, contains 43 unique Tesla reports, up from 22 in July. Four are Cybercabs:

Those are minor. Two weren’t Tesla’s fault at all, and none involved an injury.

The second bucket is the Level 2 ADAS file, which covers driver-assist systems like Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” (Supervised). Tesla has been testing Cybercabs fitted with steering wheels and a human behind them, often in places where it has no Robotaxi permit. Those crashes land in the ADAS file, with the driver type coded “In-Vehicle (Commercial / Test)” and the system “Verified Engaged.”

There are four of them, all in September 2026:

Tesla redacted the narrative of all four as confidential business information, so there’s no way to tell from the public data who was at fault or what the system was doing. Pennsylvania State Police, Austin Police, Lehi Police, and Florida Highway Patrol are listed as the investigating agencies.

The Philadelphia crash is not the Broad Street crash where a Cybercab lost its door panel that we reported in October. That one happened on a city street in October. This one happened on a highway in September, at around 10 p.m. local time.

Tesla has no permit to run automated vehicles in Pennsylvania, and it doesn’t run Robotaxi in Utah either. In Utah, a Cybercab was photographed in Park City in September with a driver visible behind the wheel.

Two of the eight Cybercab crashes involved injuries. Both are in the Level 2 file.

Across all 43 Tesla Robotaxi reports in the ADS file, the highest pre-crash speed is 29 mph. That was a driverless Model Y with two riders hitting a pothole in Dallas in September, after which one rider said they sought medical care. The median speed across all 43 reports is 1 mph.

Not one of those 43 crashes happened on a highway. Tesla coded 21 on streets, 15 in parking lots, and 7 at intersections.

Those numbers say more about where Tesla lets the system drive than about the software itself. As we reported last month, Robotaxi sticks to low-speed routes inside small geofenced zones and largely stays off highways.

The Robotaxi Safety Report Tesla published on October 21 claims zero people injured by Robotaxi over 3,112,541 driverless miles between January 22 and October 18. It doesn’t mention the Cybercab’s test fleet, and it excludes every mile driven with a safety monitor on board.

Take the speed cap off and the picture changes.

In the Level 2 data, Teslas with Autopilot or FSD engaged regularly crash at highway speeds. Our master dataset of Tesla’s ADAS reports holds 69 fatal crashes. Among the 52 where Tesla recorded a speed, the median was 53 mph, the same speed the Cybercab was going in Philadelphia, and 29 happened at 50 mph or more.

Today alone, we matched three fatal crashes to Tesla’s latest filings:

Engagement within 30 seconds of a crash, which is what triggers these reports, doesn’t prove the system caused it. But the pattern is consistent. At low speeds in a tight geofence, Tesla’s crashes are scrapes with chains, curbs, and potholes. At highway speeds, they can kill.

The Cybercab test fleet is where those two worlds overlap. It’s the same vehicle Tesla runs driverless in Austin, and the one Cybercab crash on record at real speed happened at 53 mph on a Philadelphia highway.

The Cybercab’s four driverless crashes are minor, and some weren’t Tesla’s fault. No one is denying that. But minor crashes still count, and so do the four Level 2 crashes that Tesla’s “zero injuries” framing leaves out. Both datasets describe the same vehicle running Tesla’s self-driving software.

It's looked to me for a while now that many of the improvements that people feel when they use FSD is not just the system getting better, but Elon pulling off the guardrails so the system attempts to do more stuff.

What the data shows is that Tesla has a speed problem. Its Robotaxi service looks clean largely because Tesla keeps it slow, off highways, and inside small zones. That’s also what makes it far less useful than a real ride-hailing service. You can’t take a Cybercab to the airport if the airport is on the other side of a freeway.

To be clear, we think Tesla is right to do it this way. Given what the Level 2 data shows at 50+ mph, letting driverless Cybercabs onto highways today would be reckless.

But it means the hard part is still ahead. Highways, larger geofences, and higher speeds are where crashes become fatal, and that’s where Tesla needs its system to be nearly perfect before it can scale. The Cybercab’s test crashes suggest it isn’t there yet. The question is how long Tesla can keep growing a robotaxi network that can’t go fast.

#4357. Adding wind cuts solar + battery storage power costs nearly 20%

Solar and battery storage can do a lot of the heavy lifting in a renewable electricity system. Add wind, and supplying reliable power gets nearly 20% cheaper, according to new analysis from energy think tank Ember.

Wind fills gaps when solar output drops, so the system needs fewer batteries to keep electricity flowing.

Ember’s analysis, produced with the Global Wind Energy Council (GWEC), found that adding wind to solar and battery storage cuts the median cost of meeting 90% of electricity demand from $105 to $86 per megawatt-hour.

The median cost of solar and wind power covering all demand is $89/MWh, with batteries and a little backup.

Solar and wind don’t follow the same schedule. Their output varies by time of day and across seasons, allowing one to offset the other’s shortfalls.

That matters because storing enough electricity to get through a long stretch of weak solar output gets expensive. Wind reduces the amount of energy the batteries need to store in the first place.

In the US, adding wind reduces the modeled battery requirement to meet 90% of demand from 20 hours of electricity use to 12 hours. Europe sees the same reduction, while China’s requirement falls from 18 hours to 12.

The savings also put cheaper renewable power within reach of more regions. With wind included, regions that account for 75% of global electricity demand can meet 90% of their electricity demand at less than $100/MWh. With solar and batteries alone, that share is only 50%.

“We already know that solar and wind are cheap,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember.

By combining solar, wind, and batteries, we can deliver reliable power at remarkably low costs almost everywhere in the world. That’s a pretty fundamental shift in the economics of energy.

The researchers also looked at prolonged periods of low output. Globally, weighted by electricity demand, a week of low solar output occurs roughly four times a year. A week in which both solar and wind output are low occurs only about once every four years.

That’s a global average, so individual locations will have different experiences. Ember defines a lull as seven consecutive days of output below half the source’s average.

Combining wind and solar reduces the gaps in low output.

The findings also raise questions for developers planning new fossil fuel plants.

Ember identifies 845 GW of coal and gas capacity in planning worldwide. Adding wind raises the share located in regions where solar, wind, and battery storage can meet 90% of demand for under $100/MWh from 71% to 90%.

In China alone, wind brings another 91 GW of planned coal and gas capacity into the range where renewables are cheaper.

Include backup to cover all demand, and 706 GW of the planned fossil fuel capacity sits in regions where the renewable-based alternative costs less than $100/MWh. Without wind, that figure falls to 520 GW.

For investors financing fossil fuel plants in the pipeline that are expected to run for decades, there is likely already a cheaper renewable alternative available to meet the same electricity demand, so it’s worth scrutinizing the project’s economics.

This works even better with greater efficiency on the consumption side of the equation.

Ember’s interactive Wind + Solar + Battery Atlas lets users explore reliable electricity costs in their own region.

#4356. BMW Just Started Making EV Batteries In America. The New iX5 Will Be First In Line

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

BMW’s first high-voltage battery factory for electric vehicles in the United States is now up and running in Woodruff, South Carolina. The facility, which is located just 15 miles from the automaker’s car factory in Spartanburg, will supply finished battery packs for no fewer than six Neue Klasse EVs assembled in the U.S., starting with the new iX5 SUV.

According to BMW, the new facility doesn’t build cells from scratch. Instead, it sources ready-made cells from local suppliers, which are then checked at the plant under a “zero-defect” policy. BMW is currently sourcing Gen6 cylindrical cells from AESC in China, but that will change toward the end of the decade, when LG Energy Solution will become the U.S. supplier, while Samsung SDI will supply European factories.

BMW EV battery factory in Woodruff, South Carolina

After analyzing each incoming cell for voltage and other parameters, the factory starts the clustering process, where the battery cells are connected to coolers to ensure optimal insulation and cooling. While the packs go down the assembly line, they are continuously monitored in real time to make sure that each pack goes out the door in tip-top condition.

The company’s latest EV batteries are built using the “cell-to-pack” technique, where cells are no longer arranged in modules. Instead, they’re put directly into the pack enclosure, where they’re protected by a hardened foam. This way, more cells can fit into the same volume, leading to more energy density and more driving range.

In South Carolina, all production staff go through a virtual reality training program, so they can practice real manufacturing operations under realistic conditions before they set foot on the assembly line. What’s more, BMW is relying heavily on artificial intelligence-powered digital assistants and more than 250 robots to output zero-defect batteries. Over 300 employees are currently working at the company’s new battery-making facility.

The Woodruff plant is BMW’s fourth site in its Gen6 battery production network to start series production, after the facilities in Debrecen, Hungary, Irlbach-Straßkirchen, Germany, Shenyang, China, and San Luis Potosí, Mexico.

It took the automaker roughly three years to go from groundbreaking to mass production in South Carolina. Construction of the Woodruff plant began in September 2023, and just one year later, in September 2024, the first manufacturing equipment was installed. In summer 2025, the first pre-series batteries rolled off the assembly line.

What makes the new facility special, besides being BMW’s first battery plant in the U.S., is that during normal operation, it doesn’t use any fossil fuels, with the site’s industrial trucks being powered by hydrogen. As for the latest Gen6 cylindrical cells, they’re touted as having 28% fewer carbon dioxide emissions compared to the cells used in the outgoing iX SUV.

#4355. Over 1 Million Hondas Are Being Investigated for Start-Stop Failures

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has gotten hundreds of complaints that engines are not restarting after coming to a stop at traffic lights.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) has launched an investigation into Honda’s automatic engine start-stop system. The inquiry comes after NHTSA received hundreds of complaints, with owners stating that their engines were failing to automatically restart after coming to a full stop at a traffic light.

The investigation was announced on Friday, November 13, and covers 1,033,632 total vehicles. The affected models are the Honda Passport, Odyssey, Pilot, and Ridgeline, along with the Acura MDX, all from between the 2024 and 2026 model years.

See all results for new 2026 Honda Passport for sale near 56301

In total, NHTSA’s Office of Defects Investigation has been sent 701 complaints about the automatic start-stop feature. The system is supposed to automatically turn off the engine when the vehicle comes to a complete stop, and it’s supposed to automatically restart the engine when the driver takes their foot off the brake pedal. However, “the complaints allege that the engines are failing to restart once they have been shut off by this system.” NHTSA says that there have been no injuries related to the stop-start system problems.

This isn’t the first time that this issue has arisen with Honda’s automatic start-stop system, which is meant to improve fuel economy by limiting idle time. In 2025, the federal government investigated the system, looking at 2.2 million units of the Pilot, Odyssey, Passport, Ridgeline, MDX, and Acura TLX. The previous investigation covered all of the vehicles in the current investigation, except for the 2026 model year.

Although the system failure is similar in both populations, “the vehicles in this current investigation appear to have different root causes and respond differently to repairs,” NHTSA says. More information should continue to emerge as NHTSA continues its investigation.

#4354. Battlefield 6 gets a new map today alongside major changes to controller aim assist, and even more weapon dispersion tweaks

Right on schedule, the latest Battlefield 6 patch has arrived to kick off the next stage of Season 1.

Battlefield 6’s first season has entered its second phase. The game received a major update earlier today, version 1.1.2.0, which delivers a host of changes to the game, many of which have been expected.

The update, of course, also adds new content to the game in the form of the map Eastwood, as well as new hardware and fresh features for the multiplayer sandbox.

We’ve known about the new content side of today’s patch for quite some time. The update kicks off the California Resistance stage of Season 1, which is the second of three. The new Eastwood map takes place in California, and it’s a map cut from the larger Battlefield Redsec battle royale map of Fort Lyndon.

There’s a new limited-time mode called Sabotage - a tactical, 8v8 mode where two teams attempt to destroy as many bomb sites as possible. The other big new feature that arrives today is Battle Pickups.

These are powerful weapons which can be found in specific game modes (and in Portal), scattered around the map for players to pick up and use. They have limited ammo that cannot be replenished, and deliver incredible firepower.

Redsec players have a new Gauntlet mission to look forward to that joins the existing modes. It’s called Rodeo and it involves a lot of vehicular action. Finally, everyone gets to unlock two new weapons: the the DB-12 shotgun, and the M327 Trait revolver sidearm. There’s also a new angled grip attachment.

The fixes and tweaks side of the patch is arguably the more interesting. Controller aim assist has received a big overhaul that essentially resets everything to open beta settings. The goal is to make infantry targeting more consistent.

Controller players actually get the bulk of the changes in this update, which also improves input latency and stick response. Several issues that reset aim assist values, or make it behave erratically, have been addressed.

The conversation around weapon bloom/spread doesn’t look like it’s ever going to end, because Battlefield Studios is yet again tuning gunplay to fix unintended dispersion behaviour, and decrease its intensity across the board.

Certain Challenges have had their description rewritten so their requirements can be better understood. Beyond that, you can expect several deployables to behave much more consistently, including several bug fixes there, too.

Head to the official blog for the full rundown of patch 1.1.2.0.

#4352. Tesla Model 3 Maintenance Guide: What Needs Servicing And What Doesn't

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Everybody knows that electric cars are pretty easy on the owner’s wallet when it comes to regular maintenance. They may cost more to buy new than a comparable gas car, but as the miles pile on, there’s no need to worry about engine oil changes and emissions checks. Plus, cheap EVs are already here, with more to come in the near future.

While all of this is true, EVs aren’t exactly maintenance-free. There are still some things that need to be done to keep an electric car running like new for many years after it rolled off the assembly line.

There might not be an engine under the hood, and no manual or automatic transmission to worry about, but EVs still have transmissions, believe it or not. They also have brake fluid, brake pads, and coolant. And all of these—plus others—need attention over the course of a car’s life.

ERANGE EV tires are purpose-built for electric vehicles, combining efficiency, comfort and performance with advanced EcoPoint3 technology.

For this first installment of our new series on EV maintenance, I’ll focus on the Tesla Model 3, one of the best-selling electric models of all time, and a regular occurrence on roads everywhere in the United States, Europe, and beyond.

I’ll go through what maintenance is required by Tesla to keep the warranty intact, and also discuss items that are not part of the company’s service schedule but might still be worth considering for the long run.

The following list may seem a little too simple for someone who has switched from a gas or diesel car to an EV, but there’s no shortage of high-mileage electric cars out there, including countless Teslas, that are still going strong with minimal maintenance. Here’s what Tesla recommends owners look out for on the Model 3:

High-Efficiency Particulate (HEPA) filter and carbon filter replacement: every three years, for vehicles that have them from the factory

Similar to a combustion vehicle, the Tesla Model 3 uses brake fluid to push the brake pads onto the rotors. Brake fluid is hygroscopic, meaning it naturally absorbs moisture from the air. If there’s a lot of moisture contamination, hydraulic pressure drops, which leads to a softer brake pedal and longer braking distances. A brake fluid test reveals if it’s still good or if it needs replacing.

Even though all modern EVs use their electric motors to slow down, they still rely on mechanical brakes to increase safety, and the Model 3 is no different. To keep things running smoothly, Tesla recommends cleaning and lubricating the brake calipers, especially for cars that live in areas where the roads are salted during the winter.

The thickness of the brake pads also needs to be checked, though there have been plenty of cases out there of Tesla EVs with over 100,000 miles on the clock and the original brake pads still in good condition.

Yes, the Model 3 doesn’t have a hot engine, but it still needs a radiator to keep the thermal system running cool. Depending on where the car is located, debris can build up over time, reducing the radiator’s efficiency and limiting the car’s performance.

Tesla Model 3 windshield camera precision cleaning

Tesla’s advanced driver assistance systems rely on video cameras to react, but they can’t perform as intended if they’re obstructed. The company says that cleaning the inside of the windshield in the camera area is vital for clear visibility and optimal camera function.

To check if cleaning is required, owners can tap the Maintenance tab in the infotainment system.

EVs are known for being harder on tires than gas cars because acceleration and brake regeneration will put stress on the rubber. To prolong the life of a tire set, Tesla recommends rotating the tires every 6,250 miles.

This is also when you want to check the tires themselves. Because EVs often wear out tires quicker, it's important to keep an eye on tread depth. When it gets below 4/32nds of an inch, it's time to start looking for new tires. If your tread depth is below 2/32nds, replace them immediately.

If the driver notices vibrations in the steering wheel while driving, the wheels may need balancing. With unbalanced tires, handling, tire life, and steering components are affected.

If the vehicle pulls to one side when the steering wheel is straight, or if there’s uneven wear on the tires, a wheel alignment may be needed. The procedure is also recommended after installing new tires.

All of the vehicle’s maintenance needs can be viewed in the Maintenance Summary on the central touchscreen, which provides a record of when common actions were last performed and recommends when to perform them next.

Tesla says that all of these items need to be performed at an authorized service center. This includes servicing the low-voltage and high-voltage batteries. However, there are some maintenance actions that should be considered by owners who want to treat their EVs as their forever cars.

We’ve all heard of “lifetime fluids,” but ask any well-versed mechanic out there, and they’ll say that they don’t exist. Instead, car manufacturers refer to them when it’s their job to maintain the car under warranty. After the warranty expires, the owner is on the hook for all repairs, including those that could have been avoided.

The following recommendations are nowhere to be found in Tesla’s maintenance plan, but some technicians still recommend them. Even though they’re not required actions, Tesla has service procedures for all of them, and its service centers can perform them if the owner asks.

Tesla used to recommend changing the transmission fluid in its drive units every 100,000 miles, but that went the way of the dodo. Now, the company’s transmissions, which transfer power from the electric motor to the wheels, have built-in filters, but plenty of mechanics out there believe that it’s good practice to renew the fluid every 100,000 miles at the latest.

The Model 3 uses coolant to keep the high-voltage battery at an optimal temperature. Just like on a combustion car, the coolant needs to be checked and replaced if it becomes contaminated.

Over time, rubber bushes will lose their elasticity or even crack. If this happens, knocks or rattles will make their presence felt, requiring a visit to a service center. Even though Tesla implemented many manufacturing novelties over time, it still hasn’t figured out how to replace the age-old rubber bushes found in all cars.

Under warranty, Tesla's authorized service centers should handle all maintenance items. However, after the warranty expires, many of the maintenance actions found on this list can be easily done at home by the owner. Air filter changes and radiator cleaning are DIY jobs that shouldn't take hours to complete, even for people who haven't done any mechanical work before.

Best of all, though, Tesla has published all of its service manuals online, and anyone can follow the service procedures to do maintenance jobs. What's more, in recent years, plenty of independent EV shops have popped up, and they can usually handle repairs and maintenance at lower costs than Tesla. That said, Tesla's own shops will happily inspect and repair older models, too.

Keeping an EV on the road should be much cheaper than a gas car, but it still requires some maintenance. Over a five-year period, the main maintenance items should include at least one set of new tires, multiple tire rotations, two brake fluid tests and maybe one flush, two cabin air filter replacements, several brake checks, and at least one set of wiper blades.

#4351. M3 Goes EV! We Drive a Prototype as the M Car Undergoes a Monumental Change

With four motors making around 838 horsepower, the 2027 BMW M3 prototype is a monster on the track.

Most BMW fans cannot help falling all over themselves when a new M3 is launched, but this time they might get well and truly tripped up. That’s because what BMW is calling “the fastest and most powerful BMW M3 of all time” is 100 percent electric. There’s no mention of a gasoline version and no special EV designation tagged onto the name, just “here’s the new 2027 BMW M3, and we hope you like it,” or words to that effect.

After driving a camouflaged prototype and hearing all the dirty details at BMW’s Miramas test center in southern France, we most certainly do.

This machine has four electrically excited synchronous motors, one for each wheel. The pair at each axle is not quite what you expect, with one motor situated ahead of the other and a reduction gear for one of them on each side of the shared housing. The front-axle motors make approximately 644 horsepower and 398 pound-feet of torque, while the pair on the rear axle is good for about 751 horsepower and 738 pound-feet. Combined output is likewise still subject to an asterisk at this pre-production stage, but total power is at least 838 horsepower, and torque is an axle-twisting 885 pound-feet. If you’re thinking the sum total is less than the two axles, you are absolutely correct. The surplus is there to allow for serious torque vectoring, both front to rear and side to side. In normal driving, the car operates strictly in rear-wheel drive, with the front axle brought in whenever there’s acceleration, if the situation demands front-axle recuperation, or if you have the drivetrain set to Sport mode.

See all results for new 2028 BMW M3 EV for sale near 97124

Four motors require precise and rapid control during acceleration and braking, but they also play an outsize role in cornering. It all operates much more smoothly and immediately than any electronically controlled differential or transfer case ever could, so you absolutely get what you request. The so-called Heart of Joy (essentially another name for the M Dynamic Performance Control module) is the single ECU that oversees everything in the powertrain and driving dynamics arena. It’s the brain that seamlessly decides what motor is required for whatever demands you place on the car by looking at steering position, accelerator input, and braking demands, with a nod toward the basic settings that you have dialed in.

The battery that powers all of this is specific to the M3, even though it fits in a similarly sized case as the one in the i3. It’s designed to give higher peak and sustained power output and is capable of higher energy recuperation (up to 540 kilowatts) and faster charging (420 kilowatts), which means it has a higher level of cooling. The battery capacity is slightly lower for all this, currently sitting at about 100 kWh. Estimated EPA range is currently 300 miles or so, but all of these numbers are subject to change. As for the difference between how this battery pack is installed versus the i3’s, the M3 gains a direct connection to the front and rear axle subframes for enhanced torsional rigidity for more precise handling.

See all results for new 2028 BMW M3 EV for sale near 97124

Whatever the underlying mumbo jumbo, we can say that it really works, and the result is simply epic. We first went out in the default mode, with the drivetrain, chassis, steering, and brakes set to Comfort and energy recovery set to Mid, just to get a feel of the track. Once we knew where we were going, we let fly with the M1 button, and that brought everything to Sport mode but left the energy recovery in Mid and, crucially, left the DSC stability control setting in On. We pressed the car hard, and the M3 absolutely responded, and our pace built immensely. But that eventually resulted in a bit too much understeer as speeds climbed, which led to a brief off-track excursion, as they say in the business. We kept on going, but the car was imposing a limit on our fun.

We did what you would do at that point and duly selected the M2 button. That setting was programmed by our hosts to bring the drivetrain and chassis up to Sport+ and raised the recuperation to Max. It also put the DSC in a more permissive state, otherwise known as MDM, and all of that was the magic bullet. The car now dived toward apexes and slithered nicely out of corners. The front end was quite pointy, and the rear now had permission to loosen up. Our lap times fell, and our grin widened. This car felt alive. It really did feel like an M3, just like no other before it. Through it all, the braking response felt entirely natural, probably because on the track there was a strong base level of recuperation, overlaid with a thin veneer of friction braking for a precise feel of what is happening underfoot.

Interestingly, there is a sound accompanying all of this, although BMW says it’s not modeled on any particular car. We drove it with the eDrive set to Auto, which delivers the augmented sound of six gears known as “stages.” You don’t have to shift in this mode, and there’s no real interruption of power, but the interior sound level rises and falls as the car progresses up and down through each stage. There’s extra emphasis on powertrain load and aggression, too, so when you’re driving the M3 hard, it really does give you the auditory cues that you miss when you drive an otherwise-quiet EV. If you want a manual-like experience, you can set the eDrive accordingly, and then you’ll get shift lights, and it’ll even cut power if you don’t upshift at the right time. In the time we had, this setting was not particularly fun. We’ll table this issue for now, probably until we can get our own M3 to soak in. You can also turn the eDrive to Off, in which setting the car will just quietly amble along like any other EV, but what’s the fun in that?

The prototype’s camouflage didn’t do much to cover up the exterior of the new M3, as it was formfitting. That said, you couldn’t really get a sense of the exterior look of the car, although it was still clear that every panel below the greenhouse was different from the i3. The body is distinctly pulled out to cover the wide Michelin Pilot Sport S 6 tires. Also clear to see were the M Yellow DRLs and the track lights below them, as well as many of the carbon-fiber bits, such as the hood vents, the rockers, and the mirror housings.

It was even more difficult to see what was going on inside, as much of the interior was obscured. But you could still see some things, such as the steering wheel and its extra buttons. The top of the “wings” (because the spokes are lower down in typical Neue Klasse parlance) has two extra red buttons per side. There are the M1 and M2 buttons, but there’s also the M Setup button you use in conjunction with the touchscreen to program each one. The fourth button is interesting; press it twice to deactivate the ADAS active-safety minders. For track work, it’s nice to have one button that will do all that. The 17.9-inch central screen was obvious, but BMW had it covered much of the time, except to show the new screens that had to do with setting up the M buttons. The Panoramic Vision screen at the base of the windshield was mostly visible and mostly the same apart from fonts and the like, but for some reason the central section was blocked off.

As for what it’s called, the car’s official name is just 2027 BMW M3. Like we said, there’s no EV or Electric nomenclature tagged onto the end. As for the unofficial model code that you may be wondering about, that is ZA0. More will be divulged as we get closer to its summer 2027 launch date, including the price. We have a $90,000 placeholder, but that is subject to change. As for an ICE version, there is no official word from BMW. Stay tuned.

#4350. Battlefield 6 is getting a free trial next week with... a questionable selection of maps, but at least the modes are good

If Redsec got you hooked on Battlefield gameplay but you never experienced traditional multiplayer in Battlefield 6, there's an upcoming moment you might want to pay attention to.

Presumably as a way of marching ever forward towards its (alleged) 100 million player goal for Battlefield 6, EA has announced that the multiplayer shooter will be getting its first free trial later this month.

This is, of course, specifically for players to sample the core, paid component of the game, as the recently launched Redsec remains free-to-play. Redsec, however, offers modes like battle royale and Gauntlet, which aren’t quite the traditional Battlefield experience.

The Battlefield 6 trial arrives next Tuesday, November 25. It will run for one week, ending the following Tuesday, December 2. The trial will be available on all platforms, but won’t include all content from the full game.

Instead, players will have access to three of the game’s maps and five of its modes. Siege of Cairo will be there alongside Season 1’s two new maps: Eastwood, and Blackwell Fields. It’s not the strongest line-up of maps, considering Eastwood is already cut from the larger Fort Lyndon battle royale map that Redsec players should be quite familiar with, but it’s something.

As for modes, you can pick from Conquest, Breakthrough, Sabotage, and Team Deathmatch. Battlefield Studios didn’t say what the fifth mode is going to be, but a dedicated blog post with more information is set to arrive next week.

Beyond the trial's content itself, the timing is certainly great. Battlefield 6 just received one of its biggest patches, kicking off the second phase of its first season. So far this season, we’ve seen two new maps, several new weapons - but more importantly, solutions to problems the game’s had since launch, as well as fixes to longstanding bugs.

The miserable XP progression Battlefield 6 launched with is far more tolerable. Challenges and Assignments are much easier to understand and actually finish. The often maligned weapon dispersion has been toned down. Some of the wildest vehicle bugs have been fixed. And Portal has a host of experiences that go beyond just bot farms.

In essence, Battlefield 6 feels like its reached its 1.0 status, which makes this a great entry point for new players, even if the trial could've used more of the game's better maps.

#4349. Tesla needs wireless charging fast, or its $30,000 Cybercab can’t charge at home

Tesla is now taking orders for the $29,990 Cybercab, with the first deliveries expected in Austin next month. But there’s a problem buyers should know about: they won’t be able to charge it at home.

The Cybercab has no onboard charger, so it only takes DC fast charging. And the wireless home charging pad Tesla has been teasing since 2023 still isn’t something you can buy.

When Tesla unveiled the Cybercab in 2024, Elon Musk said it wouldn’t even have a plug. “It just goes over the inductive charger and charges,” he said on stage.

That plan didn’t survive production, or at least the current version in production. Cybercabs have a NACS charge port behind a panel in the rear bumper, and Tesla has been plugging Cybercabs into regular Superchargers in Austin since they joined the fleet.

The bigger issue is what sits behind that port. Tesla confirmed to attendees at Tesla’s Austin launch event in September that Cybercab has no onboard charger, the box that turns the AC power coming out of your wall into DC power the battery can store.

No onboard charger means no Wall Connector. No Mobile Connector on a 120V outlet, and no Level 2 station at the mall either. If it isn’t a DC fast charger, the Cybercab can’t use it.

For a robotaxi, deleting the onboard charger makes sense. It’s one less part to buy, cool, and carry around, and a fleet car spends its downtime at a depot, not in someone’s garage. Those little things help make the car more economical and efficient.

But Tesla is now selling the Cybercab to individuals.

As we reported last week, Tesla’s Cybercab autonomy agreement requires a $299 monthly subscription for the car to move at all. The same document puts charging squarely on the buyer: “You are responsible for registration, insurance, parking, charging, general cleaning and all other costs.”

It also tells owners to “keep the vehicle charged and connected so over-the-air updates can install.” Connected to what, it doesn’t say.

The Cybercab Order Agreement limits the car to NACS DC fast charging, Superchargers included. It also says only the registered owner can use the Cybercab, and only while physically present in it for the entire trip.

The subscription agreement carves out one exception: when service is due, the Cybercab “will travel autonomously, unoccupied to a Tesla service center.” Nothing similar exists for charging.

So you can’t send your Cybercab to a Supercharger at 2 a.m. while you sleep, which is the one thing a self-driving car should be great at. You’d have to ride along, sit in a two-seater at a Supercharger while it charges, and ride back home.

The obvious answer is the wireless home charger Tesla keeps promising.

Tesla first showed what looked like a wireless home charging station during its Investor Day in March 2023. Later that year, chief designer Franz von Holzhausen confirmed the project on Jay Leno’s Garage, saying owners would “just drive over the pad in your garage” to start charging.

Tesla then filed patents for the charging pad and, after the Cybercab unveiling, released a video of it charging the robotaxi at 25 kW, claiming efficiency “well above 90%.” In February, the FCC granted Tesla a waiver to use ultra-wideband radios to guide the Cybercab onto the pad.

And that’s where it stops. Tesla has never sold the pad, never priced it, and never given it a launch date. It even gave up on wireless charging for the Cybertruck last year, even though the truck shipped with the connectors for it.

With deliveries estimated for December, Tesla has about six weeks to launch a home pad if it wants the first owners to charge in their own garage.

Tesla’s own plans for Cybercab charging revolve around fleet depots. In Austin, it filed plans for a hub on St. Elmo Road with 48 V4 Supercharger stalls in a first phase and cabinets to support 80 wireless chargers in a second.

Tesla could, in theory, let private owners use it. But with the owner-presence rule, that means riding to a depot across town and waiting there. That’s a Supercharger visit with extra steps.

The other route is a home DC charger, and those exist. We covered Sigenergy’s 25 kW bidirectional DC charging module last year, which bypasses a car’s onboard charger the same way a Supercharger does. Lunar Energy also announced a 25 kW home DC charger this year, but it’s not expected until mid-2027.

Neither is a plug-and-play answer. Sigenergy’s module is built to sit inside its SigenStor home battery system, which isn’t cheap, and Tesla would have to support third-party DC charging on a car it controls this tightly. Tesla could also build its own small DC wall unit. It hasn’t announced one, but CEO Elon Musk talked about integrating one into the Powerwall for years.

This is what happens when you take a vehicle designed for a fleet and sell it to consumers to hit a deadline. And let’s be honest, charging is probably not even in the top 5 of problems with selling the Cybercab to personal owners in its current state.

Musk promised a Cybercab would be sold to a customer for under $30,000 before 2027. Technically, he’s going to make it. But on the Q3 earnings call, he also said “the vast majority” of Cybercabs will stay Tesla-owned and run as transport-as-a-service. The car was clearly engineered around that, and deleting the onboard charger is the best example.

That saved Tesla money on every unit. The cost now lands on the few people buying one.

I don't see any evidence that the production Cybercab has the onboard hardware to use such a pad. Besides the wireless receiver coil it would need some kind of charging hardware to convert the pulsed wireless charging into DC to charge the battery.

If you live in Austin next to a Supercharger, you’ll manage. But think about what Tesla is actually selling here: a self-driving car that can’t drive itself to charge, can’t charge in your garage, and needs you sitting in it at a Supercharger. That’s worse than owning a Model 3 with a Wall Connector, and it costs $299 a month on top.

The fix exists in Tesla’s labs. It has the pad, the patents, and the FCC approval. It needs to ship it as a product, ideally bundled with the car, or change the contract to let the Cybercab go charge on its own.

Will the first Cybercab owners get a wireless pad in December, or will they spend their evenings at Superchargers? And if it launches, how much will it cost? The rare few home wireless chargers that have been sold to date have been quite expensive, and the value proposition of the Cybercab, which is currently basically a $300 a month lease with a $30,000 down payment, is already pretty awful.

If you’re buying an EV, how you charge it at home matters as much as the car itself, and pairing it with rooftop solar can cut your fuel costs to nearly zero. With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. #4348. Tesla Keeps Killing Cars. Now It Wants To Build Cybercabs In Germany

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Tesla’s core lineup is shrinking as the company focuses in on robotaxis. Now, Tesla boss Elon Musk wants to take his autonomous vehicle manufacturing ambitions beyond Texas and begin Cybercab production in Germany.

The company plans to invest €3 billion ($3.3 billion) to expand its factory near Berlin, targeting production of up to one million Cybercabs. According to Reuters, Tesla intends to apply for permits before the end of the year, begin construction in the first half of 2027, and start German Cybercab production in 2029.

The news comes as Tesla keeps reducing the number of conventional cars on offer. Over the past year or so, it has retired entire models, dropped cheaper variants, and earmarked factory space for robots and robotaxis. Knowing that, the new German Cybercab plan starts to look less like an addition to Tesla’s business and more like a replacement for part of it.

The most significant departures this year were the Model S and Model X. Tesla ended both model lines and announced it would repurpose its former Fremont factory space to build Optimus humanoid robots. Granted, the S and X were aging, low-volume products, but they made Tesla look more like a traditional automaker.

The Cybertruck is next, although its departure has become a moving target. Musk initially announced a mid-2027 shutdown to free Texas factory space for Cybercabs, then extended production through the end of summer to fulfill its order backlog. But it’s still scheduled for retirement.

Not even the ubiquitous Model Y has escaped. Tesla dropped its cheapest all-wheel-drive version earlier this month, less than a year after introducing it. Buyers who want two motors must now stretch to the Premium AWD or just get the base rear-wheel-drive variant, which remains available.

Tesla isn’t abandoning human-driven cars altogether. The redesigned Roadster revealed last month is now promised for 2028, complete with thruster-assisted theatrics. After years of delays and a complete redesign, it’s still a vehicle Tesla promises to build.

Basically, the new Roadster offers spectacle, but it doesn’t fill the practical gaps left by a luxury sedan, a large SUV, and a pickup. Tesla doesn’t even seem to be interested in filling those gaps.

The Cybercab faces a different issue. Without manual controls, its usefulness depends on Tesla’s autonomous driving capabilities and permission to deploy them. In the U.S., regulators have already opened an investigation into how the vehicle complies with federal safety requirements. A German production facility doesn’t, by itself, settle where its output can operate.

Tesla’s struggle to get FSD approved in Europe shows how slow that process can be. Dutch regulators cleared the supervised system in April after more than 18 months of testing, but its rollout has since depended on individual countries granting permission. EU-wide approval remains pending, and Tesla has renamed it “Tesla Assisted Driving” and tightened its speed settings to address regulators’ concerns.

All that work is for software that still requires an attentive driver. Getting permission for a Cybercab with no steering wheel or pedals is a separate challenge. And now Tesla wants to build those in Europe…

Still, Tesla’s survival doesn’t only rest on the Cybercab. The Model 3 and Model Y are still very popular worldwide, and the Semi could give it a foothold in electric trucking. But shrinking its passenger car lineup while spending billions on robotaxis leaves Tesla with fewer alternatives if Musk’s driverless future takes longer or proves less profitable than he expects.

#4346. Volkswagen is cooking up a ‘spicy’ new electric hot hatch

Volkswagen will reveal the new GTI hot hatch on Friday, promising it will be “something really spicy.”

To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen is “starting a new chapter,” with its first all-electric model to bear the iconic performance badge.

The ID. Polo GTI “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW said after opening pre-orders last month.

Volkswagen previewed a mysterious new hot hatch draped under a cloth that appears to be a souped-up version of the ID. Polo GTI. Despite its attempt to “hide” it, you can see the massive rear wing and wide wheel arches under the cloth.

The company promised that “something really spicy” will be served this Friday, November 20, with the tags #Volkswagen, #GTI, and #GTI50.

Although no other details were revealed, the new hot hatch is thought to be the more powerful “Clubsport” variant.

A post shared by Volkswagen (@volkswagen)

Volkswagen’s head of driving dynamics, Florian Umbach, told Autocar earlier this year that the company is planning to launch the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, a more powerful variant that will deliver close to 300 hp, up from 223 hp in the standard model.

Umbach said that Volkswagen is developing “a similar kind of paddleshift power delivery that the Hyundai N cars have” for the upcoming electric hot hatch.

Hyundai’s performance EVs, the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, feature a simulated gear-shifting system called N e-Shift that uses paddle shifters on the steering wheel to replicate the feel of an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. It works with the N Active Sound+ system to make it feel like you’re in a traditional gas-powered sports car.

It has yet to be confirmed whether the hot hatch debuting on Friday is, in fact, the new ID. Polo Clubsport, but the design clues give us a good idea of what’s coming.

Man, $45k for a starting price is a little uncomfortably steep for a hatch, given there are a little bigger options in that range. I wish it started somewhere in the 30s to be competitive.

Check back on Friday for the full details.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000).

Like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the electric ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 223 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.

In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

#4345. Battlefield 6 streamlines some of the most annoying Challenges yet again, takes out a few of them entirely

The easier and more accessible Battlefield Studios makes those Battlefield 6 Challenges, the better.

The work to continue streamlining Challenges in Battlefield 6 is clearly not done. Having just released a new patch - which already included several updates to Challenges and Assignments - Battlefield Studios has gone in and made even more changes.

This latest round includes far fewer tweaks, but quite surprisingly, it also removes a few of the more annoying ones from the game.

The updated list, which Battlefield shared on Twitter, includes changes to the dreaded Recon 2 headshots beyond 150m Challenge. Now, any headshot beyond 75m will count. Recon Expert 3 is another headshot-themed one that’s been updated, and now requires getting headshot kills beyond 125m, rather than the practically impossible beyond 200m that it required previously.

The Rapid Fire 2 Challenge, which required getting kills beyond 50m with Assault Rifles, has been changed so it now tracks anything beyond 40m. The painful ‘Inflict damage under 15m while hip-firing with Assault Rifles’ has been entirely replaced with one that requires - the far more sensible - inflicting damage while in ADS with Assault Rifles.

A couple of Challenges, such as the one that required suppressing enemies with LMGs, and another that wanted you to deal damage to laser-designated vehicles using lock-on weapons, have both been removed.

The journey to make Challenges and Assignments easier to complete has been a long one. Progression has been one of the key areas of criticism Battlefield 6 received at launch. The issue encompassed more than just slow player and weapon XP earn rates, it also prevented players from accessing new Training Paths for the various classes, and several of the game's weapons.

Battlefield Studios attacked the problem from multiple angles, initially boosting the XP players and their weapons would earn, before later reducing the requirements of the Challenges themselves. The developer continued to streamline those requirements over multiple patches, including majorly overhauling the system earlier this month.

It seems the studio is more confident than ever in the game, as it recently announced that Battlefield 6 will be getting its first free trial next week, offering players who do not own the full game access to iconic modes like Conquest, and Breakthrough - though on an unusual selection of maps.

#4344. Mercedes Is Bringing Hands-Free Driving To Certain U.S. Highways In 2027

Browse this and many other websites without banner ads, personalized tracking and video ads.

Mercedes is bringing a new suite of driver assistance features. The two big new ones are Mercedes' MB.Drive Assist Pro, an FSD-like system we recently tested, and Hands-Free Highway Assist.

Silly corporate naming conventions aside, this new system is impressive. MB.Drive Assist Pro is a true point-to-point system, capable of taking you from your starting point to your destination on its own in urban environments as long as you directly supervise it. Mercedes is still calling it an SAE Level 2 system, so you still need to pay attention, keep your hands on the wheel, and take over whenever it needs. But it can do the heavy lifting for you.

On the highway, the Hands-Free Highway Assist can completely take over inputs on approved roads at speeds up to 85 mph. You'll need radar cruise engaged to use it. Once it's on, though, it can change lanes, overtake slower vehicles, handle lane merging, and even take off-ramps for you on its own, assuming the conditions are appropriate. Think of it like Super Cruise, just from Mercedes.

"By bringing hands-free highway driving together with point-to-point assistance and expanding these technologies across our portfolio, we’re making them available to more customers across the U.S.," said Jason Hoff, CEO Mercedes-Benz North America. "That’s where sophisticated technology becomes meaningful: when it makes everyday driving more comfortable and convenient.”

China has already had the system, but Mercedes is going to begin bringing it to German and the U.S. The latter of which will actually get a sneak preview of it in December, 2026, but only in California. Select Californian customers will be able to participate in an Early Access Program (EAP), which will let them test out these new features. Only lessees of the 2026/2027 Mercedes CLA, 2027 GLC Electric SUV2, S-Class Sedan, GLE SUV and Coupe, and GLS will be eligible.

Rollout for the rest of the country will happen in Spring 2027, and it will be available for all Mercedes vehicles with the proper hardware equipped. Even owners of existing vehicles with the necessary hardware will be able to buy the feature and have it digitally installed via an over-the-air update.

#4342. Aston Martin and Fernando Alonso Will Take on the 2027 Dakar Rally

Known for elegant road cars, Aston is gearing up for its first rally-raid competition, working with Prodrive on the radical Dreadnought racer.

The name Aston Martin conjures images of luxurious grand tourers flowing swiftly down curving mountain roads, perhaps with a certain British MI6 secret agent sitting suavely behind the wheel. In recent years, Aston Martin has also become increasingly involved in racing, from its Vantage-based GT3 car to Formula 1. Now, the British automaker is embarking on a new motorsports challenge, and it’s not one we were expecting: Aston Martin will compete in the 2027 Dakar Rally.

Dakar, for those unfamiliar, is one of the most grueling off-road rally races in the world. Starting in 1979, drivers originally raced from Paris, France, to Dakar, Senegal. More recently, the rally has been held in the desert of Saudi Arabia, departing its original location after violence in Mauritania. Now, the tension in the Middle East caused by the war between the United States and Iran has forced the Dakar Rally to move once again.

See all results for used Aston Martin for sale near 51503

Aston Martin’s first Dakar will see the fledgling outfit run from Loulé, Portugal, to Marrakesh, Morocco. Although this is Aston Martin’s first time entering the Dakar Rally, it has found a well-versed partner in Prodrive. The British racing and engineering company developed the BRX Hunter, which ran from 2021 to 2024, managing a best finish of second, before partnering with Dacia to create the Sandrider, which ran in 2025 and 2026, triumphing at last year’s event.

Prodrive and Aston Martin already work together on endurance GT racing, so it’s not a shock that Aston Martin collaborated with Prodrive to develop and build the new Dreadnought rally raid car. This rally challenger borrows its name from an SUV designed by Aston Martin for the recently launched Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 video game, and it shares some design elements with the virtual off-roader.

The front end is characterized by a pair of octagonal lights that mirror the square pixel lighting from the video-game SUV. Like the Sandrider, the spare tires are tucked into the bodywork just behind the rear doors. Around back, the slatted roof, tall ducktail spoiler, and intricate LED lighting carry over from the Call of Duty Dreadnought. No technical details were revealed about the Dakar racer just yet, but we wouldn’t be surprised if the Aston Martin shares some components with the Sandrider, just as it was an evolution of the BRX Hunter. A new engine is likely—the Hunter used a Ford twin-turbo 3.5-liter V-6 and the Dacia used a Nissan twin-turbo 3.0-liter V-6—but we don’t know what Aston Martin and Prodrive settled on, although a Mercedes-Benz V-6 seems likely.

See all results for used Aston Martin for sale near 51503

Aston Martin has also amassed an incredible lineup of drivers for the race. Two-time Formula 1 World Champion and current Aston Martin F1 driver Fernando Alonso will take a break from driving on pavement to pilot one of the three Dreadnoughts. Alonso has competed in the Dakar Rally once before, taking a Toyota Hilux race truck to 13th place in 2020.

The second car will be driven by Sébastien Loeb, a nine-time World Rally champion who has finished second three times at the Dakar. Loeb is extremely familiar with Prodrive machinery, spending the last six years driving the BRX Hunter and the Dacia Sandrider. Last but not least, Aston Martin has signed Lucas Moraes, the 2025 World Rally Raid champion who has a best finish at Dakar of third, to drive the third Dreadnought.

The 2027 Dakar Rally kicks off on January 9 and runs over 12 stages until January 23. The competitors will cover a total of 4228 miles, with 2600 miles consisting of special stages, the timed portion of the event that occurs over the most challenging terrain. While Aston Martin will be a fresh face in the Dakar bivouac, a seasoned group of drivers and a successful partner in Prodrive give the new team promise when the rally kicks off in two months.

JLR's all-electric baby Defender is coming soon. According to Car and Driver, JLR boss PB Balaji recently said on an earnings call that the smaller, all-electric Defender will go into production at the end next year, alongside the upcoming Range Rover GT. There's no official name for the bite-sized Defender, but Balaji reportedly didn't want to call it the Defender Sport.

While JLR didn't give much info on what the electric baby Defender will be, we do know that it will be built on the same Electrified Modular Architecture (EMA) platform that underpins the Range Rover GT. So it makes sense that it'll be built at the same factory. That factory currently builds the existing piston-powered Discovery Sport and the Range Rover Evoque. So JLR is basically just replacing the current combustion cars with their new electric counterparts.

Despite both cars being built in the same factory, Balaji seemed to suggest that only the Defender will go into production in 2027. There's not much word on any technical specs just yet, but EMA supports 800-volt architectures and is capable of housing both pure battery-electric powertrains and hybrids. The baby Defender could very well offer both, but whichever powertrain it has, it'll need to be capable off-road to deliver on its name.

According to Motor1, Mark Cameron, managing director of Defender and Discovery brands, said "We have got to make sure everything we do as Defender has the DNA of the brand: epic built-to-last, go-anywhere capability."

Pricing, specs, and range are all still under wraps, although it might make sense for either new electric product to have the same 118.5-kWh battery as the current Range Rover Electric. With it, the electric Rover is capable of 333 miles of range, and that uses a conventional platform. The battery is also capable of 350 kW DC fast-charging, which would be very competitive in the segment, so it might make sense for JLR to roll with that battery tech. The big Range Rover Electric has a dual-motor powertrain, with 542 horsepower, but that might be a bit much for a baby Defender. Although, there could be a go-fast version with that much power, similar to the current Defender Octa.

Land Rover pushed the current full-size Defender's electric replacement out to sometime in the 2030s, so there shouldn't be any confusion between the full-size and bite-size models. If production begins in late 2027, that means we could see the baby Defender soon.

#4340. Arc Raiders patch nerfs the Deadline mine, ends the menace of the Venator

The first post-Stella Montis patch for Arc Raiders has arrived, and it predictably touches much of what people brought to the latest map.

Arc Raiders has received a new update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance issues with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

In today’s update, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

The patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

This change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

#4339. Tesla unveils 7.4 MW Powercore to take on ex-exec Baglino’s Heron Link

Tesla has unveiled Powercore, a solid-state medium-voltage transformer that also handles the inverter and breaker functions in a single unit. Tesla rates it at 7.4 MW (9 MVA) continuously at 34.5 kV, with grid-forming support up to 10 MVA of peak power.

It’s made in America and scheduled to start operating in 2027. That’s the same year Heron Power, the startup founded by Tesla’s former top engineer Drew Baglino, plans to start volume production of its own solid-state transformer, the Heron Link.

Update: Tesla has since released a full spec sheet for Powercore, including efficiency, warranty, and its data center plans. We’ve updated the article with the new details.

Tesla first said it would build its own transformers in September 2025, when it unveiled Megapack 3 and Megablock. Megablock connects four Megapack 3 units to a transformer and switchgear, but Tesla shared next to nothing about the transformer itself.

Powercore is that missing piece. Tesla announced it today through its Tesla Megapack account on X:

Introducing PowercoreSolid state medium voltage transformer, inverter and breaker – reliable, safe and secure7.4 MW/9 MVA continuously at 34.5 kVac w/ grid-forming support for 10MVA of peak powerMade in America. Operating 2027 pic.twitter.com/sHxqnpWJrf

About an hour later, Tesla followed up with a much longer post on X laying out the full spec sheet:

It also packs a built-in solid-state medium-voltage breaker that Tesla says clears faults up to 1,000x faster than a conventional breaker. There’s no flammable oil, and it’s modular, so components can be serviced in the field without swapping the whole unit.

Tesla is pitching one product for three markets: battery storage, utility-scale solar, and 800 Vdc data centers. For Megablock, Powercore replaces the current two-step setup, where Megapack’s inverters output 480 V AC before a separate transformer steps it up to medium voltage. Tesla says that old architecture had twice the losses. For solar, Powercore works as a central inverter for today’s 1,500 Vdc arrays and upcoming 2,000 Vdc systems.

Tesla still hasn’t shared pricing, customers, or a factory location. It only says Powercore will be made in the US “of U.S. and imported parts” with first units operating in 2027.

The idea behind a solid-state transformer is simple enough. A typical solar or battery project uses low-voltage inverters to convert DC into AC, then a big oil-filled, iron-core transformer to step that up to grid voltage. A solid-state unit does both jobs with silicon carbide power electronics, which means less gear, a smaller footprint, and active control over voltage and frequency. That control is what “grid-forming” means: the unit can help hold the grid steady instead of just following it.

And with lead times on conventional transformers stretching into years as data centers and renewable projects pile into interconnection queues, there’s real demand for an alternative.

You can’t look at Powercore without thinking of Heron Power.

Baglino spent 18 years at Tesla and finished as SVP of powertrain and energy, in charge of batteries, motors, power electronics, and energy products. He left in April 2024 and launched Heron Power in 2025 to build solid-state transformers.

He brought a lot of Tesla’s power electronics talent with him. As we reported when Tesla first announced its transformer plans, Heron hired engineers who led power electronics design for Powerwall 3, the next-gen Megapack, and Superchargers, along with the person who ran Tesla’s power electronics controls team for charging and energy products.

Since then, Heron has raised a $38 million Series A, a $140 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz and Breakthrough Energy Ventures, and a $60 million credit facility from J.P. Morgan and TriplePoint Capital. Former Tesla CFO Zach Kirkhorn sits on its board, and Tesla co-founder JB Straubel is an investor.

It’s also building Heron Factory One, a 286,000-square-foot plant in Morgan Hill, California, designed to make 10,000 Heron Links a year. That’s over 40 GW of annual capacity, with commercial production planned for late 2027.

And the customers are lining up. Vantage reserved more than 1 GW for its data centers, Intersect reserved 1.5 GW, LG Energy Solution Vertech is integrating Heron Link with its US-made battery systems, and RWE signed a pilot to install Heron Links at a Texas battery storage site in April 2027. Baglino says Heron has 50 GW of orders in the pipeline.

Here’s how the two compare based on what each company has disclosed:

On paper, Powercore is the bigger box, and now it has the better numbers too. At 7.4 MW continuous, it carries about 50% more power per unit than the 5 MW Heron Link, and its 98.86% peak efficiency edges out Heron’s 98.6%. But Tesla’s figure is a peak number, and Heron doesn’t label its own as one, so it’s not quite apples to apples. Neither company has shared pricing.

Tesla is also going straight at Heron’s data center pitch. Powercore converts medium voltage directly to 800 Vdc, the rack architecture Nvidia is pushing, and Tesla says it’s working with Nvidia on 800 Vdc designs. Heron’s data center version does the same 34.5 kV AC to 800 VDC conversion with built-in storage, and data centers make up about a third of its business. Tesla’s answer to the storage piece is Megapack on the DC bus, and it says it already has 10 GWh of Megapack running at data centers.

A big chunk of the people who designed Tesla’s power electronics over the last decade now work at Heron, and the guy who ran the whole org is its CEO. Tesla’s energy business also lost its longtime leader, Mike Snyder, last month, according to the WSJ.

This is all wrong. Tesla started developing this 3 years ago. Before Heron. The team selling Powercore is same as Megapack that has a way larger customer base than Heron. Also Heron is not a bankable company per project finance terms. So they will struggle to get projects financed through equity and senior debt . Not as Tesla

To be fair, Tesla still has plenty of power electronics expertise. Its silicon carbide inverters are in millions of cars and every Megapack. And it has something Heron doesn’t: a massive installed base and a sales channel. Tesla says it’s almost sold out of Megapacks for 2027, and bundling Powercore into Megablock is an easy upsell. Plenty of developers will take the one-stop shop.

Tesla’s specs now match or beat Heron’s on paper. But Heron has named customers, a pilot site with an install date, and a factory under construction. Tesla has none of those yet. I wouldn’t be surprised if Heron is actually ahead here.

But either way, the transformer shortage is big enough for both companies to sell everything they can build.

#4338. 2028 Ford Mustang GTD

See all results for new 2028 Ford Mustang GTD for sale near 48105

The Blue Oval's most famous stallion has historically been a sports car for the masses, but the Ford Mustang GTD isn't for the faint of heart or pocket. For all intents and purposes, the GTD is an IMSA GT3 racecar for the road, but with far more power. Sandwiched between its flared-and- vented front fenders, a supercharged V-8 sends 815 racehorses sprinting through an eight-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission. For reference, the Mustang GT3 race cars that compete in IMSA and at Le Mans only make around 550 horsepower.

Earth-quaking power is only one of the GTD's tricks, though, and with advanced active aerodynamics, a racing-derived pushrod rear suspension setup, and carbon-fiber bodywork, Ford's super pony can beat all production cars but Mercedes's AMG One hypercar around the Nürburgring Nordschleife. While the racetrack is undeniably the GTD's natural habitat, it's also surprisingly civilized on the road. That combination of traits, and an ultra-limited production run, makes the GTD a rare breed with a six-digit price tag to match.

Expert Tip: If you're after a lightning-fast palomino but can't quite justify the GTD's retirement-draining price tag, the Ford Mustang Darkhorse SC is well worth looking into. The SC might not have the GTD's trick suspension, but it features a virtually identical supercharged Predator 5.2-liter V-8 that churns out 795 horsepower.

Ford has a few changes in store for the GTD in 2028. A new 1901 special edition has joined the lineup, replacing last year’s Spirit of America model. The 1901 features special Royal Red exterior paint and Mahogany Red leather. Ford hasn’t released pricing information for the 1901, but says that production will be extremely limited.

After encountering manufacturing issues earlier in the GTD's build cycle, magnesium wheels are finally available. The company claims that the new wheels save 50.3 pounds of unsprung mass, which should positively impact handling.

In addition to the new wheels, the GTD's paddle shifters have been redesigned and are now 3D printed from titanium. An additional stripe design has also been added to the order sheet, and the Liquid Carbon special edition now comes with teal accenting.

Car and Driver calculates your car's value in three free and easy steps - using the same Black Book® data dealers use to appraise vehicles.

With 815 horsepower from its supercharged Predator 5.2-liter V-8 engine, the roadgoing car has far more power than the Mustang GT3 race car it shares styling with. That track-only model instead uses a 5.4-liter V-8 with around 550 horsepower. Cog swaps for the GTD come courtesy of a rear-mounted eight-speed dual-clutch automated transaxle, similar to the type of gearbox used in the race car.

A Mustang GTD we tested blew us away with its performance. Its shockingly civilized on-road ride quality surprised us as well. We would welcome more steering feedback, but the supremely balanced handling and staggering levels of grip make for a world-class driving experience.

In Comparison: The Mustang GTD is quick, but two other rear-drive rockets, the Chevrolet Corvette ZR1 and Porsche 911 GT3 RS, outran it to 60 mph in our testing, completing that task in 2.2 and 2.7 seconds, respectively.

The Ford Mustang GTD prioritizes lap times over fuel economy, as the roar from its mighty supercharged V-8 quickly reveals. As a result, the GTD only manages a pitiful 10 mpg in the city, 17 mpg on the highway, and 12 mpg combined, according to the EPA. For more information about the Mustang GTD's fuel economy, visit the EPA's website.

First Row: Though it looks every bit like the Mustang GT3 purpose-built race car on the outside, the GTD's cabin looks a lot like any ol' Mustang's. Suede, leather, and carbon fiber are the main ingredients of the GTD's interior that upgrade it from its lesser kin—though not by much. Recaro bucket seats hug both driver and front passenger, but the GTD jettisons the rear seats of other Mustang models. The paddle shifters are 3D-printed from titanium, same for the rotary dial gear selector and serial placard. Ford claims it sourced the material for these components from retired Lockheed Martin F-22 fighter jets.

Cargo Capacity: The trunk is a treasure box of suspension and cooling components, but there is room for some small pieces of soft luggage where the rear seat used to be.

The Mustang GTD packs a 12.4-inch digital gauge cluster and a 13.2-inch touchscreen infotainment display. Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are standard equipment. Though the system is largely the same as that of other Mustangs, it does include additional GTD-exclusive performance menus.

As you'd expect of a car like this, the GTD doesn't have many driver-assistance features, but it does have a lane-keep assist system and automatic emergency braking.

For information about the GTD's crash-test results, visit the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Insurance Institute for Highway Safety (IIHS) websites.

The Mustang GTD has a solid but average warranty. However, unlike rival Chevy, Ford doesn't provide a complimentary scheduled maintenance visit.

Bentley’s first electric car, the Torcal SUV, looks like a hit already. Even though production hasn’t started yet, the $220,000+ EV is sold out for 2027, according to Frank-Steffen Wallier, the company’s head honcho, quoted by Automotive News.

The British luxury automaker said that all available production slots for next year have already been allocated and that the company is now taking orders that will be delivered in 2028. Bentley didn’t say how many EVs it will build in 2027, but the initial customer response has made the marque quite happy with the outcome.

“Needless to say, we’re very pleased with the response and position we’re in,” a company spokesperson told Automotive News.

That’s great news for Bentley, which isn’t doing great in terms of sales and profit. From January through September, it sold 5,970 cars globally, 17% fewer compared to the same period last year. Meanwhile, the profit dropped by more than half to $54.1 million through the first nine months of the year.

The Torcal, which is smaller than the Bentayga SUV, is the brand’s cheapest model, though it still costs a pretty penny. The base Torcal starts at $222,495, followed by the more powerful Torcal S at $262,695, and the Torcal First Edition at $300,995. All things considered, Walliser said that the smaller size and relatively lower price compared to the Bentayga have attracted new and younger customers to the brand.

By comparison, the Bentayga starts at $231,150, the Flying Spur sedan starts at $254,850, and the Continental GT two-door starts at $288,750.

So far, the Torcal S has proved to be the most popular version of the new EV, but when it comes to personalization, the sky’s the limit. “We see cars spec’d north of 300,000 pounds ($397,086),” said Walliser. “Individual content does not stop in case of an electric car. There have been some assumptions, and some people have been critical if people would be ready to do so.”

Based on the same underpinnings as the electric Porsche Cayenne, the Bentley Torcal is powered by a 113-kilowatt-hour battery that can be charged at up to 400 kilowatts. It can go from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes, and the estimated EPA range is expected to be over 300 miles.

Built on the Premium Platform Electric (PPE) architecture, it has two electric motors that make 810 horsepower and 881 pound-feet of torque in the standard Torcal and a whopping 876 hp and 996 lb-ft of torque in the Torcal S. When the model debuted in September, Bentley said it was the most powerful and quietest model to come out of the factory in Crewe.

To make the Torcal a reality, Bentley invested $463 million to upgrade its factory in England, plus at least the same amount for supply chain preparations and research and development, Walliser said.

Despite the electric SUV’s initial success, the British automaker is still heavily invested in gas and plug-in hybrid models, and the Bentayga isn’t going anywhere. “We have a very good combination with Torcal and Bentayga,” Walliser said. “The segment definitely has space for two cars.”
